AK.title: An Act Restoring Political Party Primaries, Ending Ranked-Choice General Elections, and Repealing Recent Campaign Finance Laws
AK.ballot_label: This act would get rid of open primary elections, where all candidates appear on one ballot. It would also get rid of ranked-choice general elections. It would bring back political party primaries and single-choice general elections. It would also repeal certain campaign finance rules that were added by a 2020 ballot measure. ... Should this initiative become law?
plain: Ends Alaska's open primary (all candidates on one ballot) and ends ranked-choice voting in general elections.
Brings back party primaries; in the general election you vote for one candidate and the one with the most votes wins.
Repeals campaign finance rules added by a 2020 ballot measure, including some donation limits and 'true source' disclosure rules.
AK.yes: A yes vote returns Alaska to party primaries and single-choice general elections and repeals the 2020 campaign finance rules.
AK.no: A no vote keeps the current top-four open primary, ranked-choice general election, and 2020 campaign finance rules.
AK.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept. 22, 2026; the state's Official Election Pamphlet is not yet released.

AK.title: An Act Addressing Voter Qualification
AK.ballot_label: Alaska law requires that someone must be a United States citizen and meet other requirements to vote. This act would specify that only those who are United States citizens and meet the other requirements may vote. This act would not change the requirements to vote. Should this initiative become law?
plain: Current law says a person who is a U.S. citizen and meets other rules may vote in any election.
This act changes the wording to say that only U.S. citizens who meet the other rules may vote.
The official summary says the act does not change who is eligible to vote.
AK.yes: A yes vote rewrites Alaska's voter qualification law to state that only U.S. citizens may vote in any election.
AK.no: A no vote leaves the current wording of the voter qualification law unchanged.
AK.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept. 22, 2026.

AZ.title: Prohibits taxes or fees based on vehicle miles traveled and laws monitoring or limiting vehicle miles traveled without consent
AZ.ballot_label: A "yes" vote shall have the effect of amending the Arizona Constitution to prohibit: (1) taxes or fees on based on motor vehicle miles traveled; and (2) laws or rules that monitor or limit motor vehicle miles traveled without consent. These prohibitions do not apply in certain instances to interstate commercial vehicles or to vehicles owned by the state or local governments.
plain: Bans state and local governments from charging any tax or fee based on how many miles a vehicle is driven.
Bans laws or rules that track or limit a person's driving miles without that person's consent.
Some exceptions apply for interstate commercial vehicles and government-owned vehicles.
AZ.yes: A yes vote adds a constitutional ban on mileage-based taxes or fees and on tracking or limiting miles driven without consent.
AZ.no: A no vote keeps the constitution as is, leaving the legislature free to adopt mileage-based taxes, fees, or monitoring rules.
AZ.fiscal: No fiscal impact statement is published; Arizona requires JLBC fiscal statements only for citizen initiatives, and this is a legislative referral.

AZ.title: Adds further details to the constitutional prohibition against preferential treatment or discrimination by the state based on race, ethnicity, or other classes
AZ.ballot_label: A "yes" vote shall have the effect of amending the Arizona Constitution's current prohibition against preferential treatment or discrimination by the state based on race, ethnicity, or other classes, to specifically prohibit: (1) compelling individuals to support preferential treatment or discrimination based on race or ethnicity as a condition of education, employment, or contract opportunities; ...
plain: Expands the constitution's existing ban on state discrimination or preferential treatment based on race or ethnicity.
Bars requiring people to endorse race-based preferences (such as DEI statements) to get education, jobs, or contracts, and bars public money for public-education jobs that promote them.
Bans discipline practices that treat students or employees differently by race or ethnicity; certain exceptions apply.
AZ.yes: A yes vote adds these specific anti-preference prohibitions to the Arizona Constitution.
AZ.no: A no vote keeps the constitution's current language on preferential treatment and discrimination unchanged.
AZ.fiscal: No fiscal impact statement is published; Arizona requires JLBC fiscal statements only for citizen initiatives, and this is a legislative referral.

AZ.title: Requires all voters, including voters who vote by mail, to show government-issued ID to vote in each election; makes other changes to election administration and campaign finance prohibitions
AZ.ballot_label: A "yes" vote shall have the effect of amending the Arizona Constitution to: (1) require voters to show proof of identity when voting in each election, including when voting by mail; (2) changing existing proof of identity requirements to limit acceptable documentation to government-issued ID; ...
plain: Every voter, including mail voters, must show proof of identity, limited to government-issued ID.
Election officials must let voters have their ballot counted at their voting location on Election Day, and foreign nationals may not spend to influence Arizona elections.
Changes the legal standard courts use to review election laws, making challenges harder, and requires the legislature to fund these changes.
AZ.yes: A yes vote amends the constitution to require government-issued ID for all voting, including by mail, and makes the other listed election changes.
AZ.no: A no vote keeps the current constitutional provisions governing elections.
AZ.fiscal: No fiscal impact statement is published; Arizona requires JLBC fiscal statements only for citizen initiatives, and this is a legislative referral (the measure itself directs the legislature to appropriate implementation funds).

AZ.title: Retroactively prohibits local governments from adopting or increasing a tax on groceries without voter approval and sets a maximum rate of 2%
AZ.ballot_label: A "yes" vote shall have the effect of: (1) retroactively prohibiting local governments from adopting or increasing a tax on groceries from July 1, 2025, through June 30, 2027; and (2) after that time, prohibiting local governments from adopting or increasing a tax on groceries without voter approval ...
plain: Cities, towns, and counties could not create or raise a grocery tax from July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2027.
After that, any new or higher local grocery tax would need voter approval.
Any new or increased local grocery tax would be capped at 2%.
AZ.yes: A yes vote blocks local grocery tax increases through mid-2027 and then requires voter approval, with a 2% cap.
AZ.no: A no vote keeps current law on local government taxation of groceries.
AZ.fiscal: No fiscal impact statement is published; Arizona requires JLBC fiscal statements only for citizen initiatives, and this is a legislative referral.

AZ.title: Declares that drug cartels are terrorist organizations; directs the Arizona Department of Homeland Security to do everything in its authority to address drug cartels
AZ.ballot_label: A "yes" vote shall have the effect of: (1) declaring drug cartels as terrorist organizations and directing the Arizona Department of Homeland Security to do everything in its authority to address threats posed by drug cartels; (2) defining "drug cartel" to mean an ongoing formal or informal association of persons engaged in human smuggling, drug trafficking ...
plain: Declares drug cartels to be terrorist organizations under Arizona law.
Directs the Arizona Department of Homeland Security to use all its authority to address cartel threats.
Defines "drug cartel" as a group engaged in human smuggling, drug trafficking, or terrorism, and says the measure does not support anyone's asylum claim.
AZ.yes: A yes vote declares drug cartels terrorist organizations and directs the state homeland security department to act against them.
AZ.no: A no vote keeps current state law on terrorism and the Arizona Department of Homeland Security.
AZ.fiscal: No fiscal impact statement is published; Arizona requires JLBC fiscal statements only for citizen initiatives, and this is a legislative referral.

AZ.title: Requires all schools and athletic associations to designate athletic teams as male, female, or coed based on the biological sex of the athletes as defined at birth; prohibits these entities from authorizing use of private spaces not designated for a person's sex
AZ.ballot_label: A "yes" vote shall have the effect of: (1) requiring private schools, public schools, and athletic associations to designate every athletic team as male, female, or coed/mixed based on sex and to prevent males from joining female teams; existing law imposes this requirement only on public schools and those competing against them; ...
plain: All public and private schools and athletic associations must label every sports team male, female, or coed based on sex and keep males off female teams; current law covers only public schools and their opponents.
Schools could not let anyone use restrooms, locker rooms, or similar private spaces not designated for their sex.
Defines "sex" by the original birth certificate and lets athletes sue schools that knowingly break the law.
AZ.yes: A yes vote extends sex-based team designations to all schools, restricts private-space use by sex, and allows athlete lawsuits.
AZ.no: A no vote keeps current state law on student athletics.
AZ.fiscal: No fiscal impact statement is published; Arizona requires JLBC fiscal statements only for citizen initiatives, and this is a legislative referral.

AZ.title: Prohibits state agencies and local governments from using photo enforcement systems for traffic enforcement unless provided by contract as of December 31, 2026; requires local governments to obtain voter approval to continue their use
AZ.ballot_label: A "yes" vote shall have the effect of: (1) prohibiting state agencies and local governments from using photo enforcement systems to identify violators of traffic laws unless the agency or government contracts to use those systems by December 31, 2026; and (2) requiring local governments to obtain voter approval of existing photo enforcement systems ...
plain: Bans new photo traffic-enforcement systems (such as red-light and speed cameras) unless a contract is in place by Dec. 31, 2026.
Local governments with existing camera systems must get voter approval at the next general election to keep using them.
Voters would have to re-approve those systems every 10 years.
AZ.yes: A yes vote blocks new traffic cameras and requires voter approval to keep existing ones.
AZ.no: A no vote keeps current law on photo traffic enforcement.
AZ.fiscal: No fiscal impact statement is published; Arizona requires JLBC fiscal statements only for citizen initiatives, and this is a legislative referral.

AZ.title: Requires certain school districts to spend at least sixty percent of their operational spending on direct instructional expenses as defined by the Auditor General; reduces certain state funding for non-compliant districts
AZ.ballot_label: A "yes" vote shall have the effect of: (1) requiring school districts with 7,500 or more students in any county or that operate in a county with 500,000 or more people to spend at least 60% of their operational spending on direct instructional expenses; (2) requiring the state Auditor General to define "operational spending" and "direct instructional expenses"; ...
plain: School districts with 7,500 or more students, or in counties with 500,000 or more people, must spend at least 60% of operating money on direct instruction.
The state Auditor General defines the terms; districts that fall short must adjust spending each year until they comply.
Non-compliant districts lose 25% of their Classroom Site Fund money each year, with limited waivers from the Superintendent of Public Instruction.
AZ.yes: A yes vote requires large school districts to put at least 60% of operating spending into direct instruction or lose some state funding.
AZ.no: A no vote keeps current law on school district budgets.
AZ.fiscal: No fiscal impact statement is published; Arizona requires JLBC fiscal statements only for citizen initiatives, and this is a legislative referral.

CO.title: Law Enforcement Communication with Federal Immigration Authorities
CO.ballot_label: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution requiring law enforcement to notify the department of homeland security when a person is charged with either a violent crime or any crime if the person has a prior felony conviction if law enforcement cannot determine that the person is lawfully present in the United States?
plain: Police, corrections officers, and district attorney staff would have to notify the U.S. Department of Homeland Security within 72 hours when they charge someone with a violent crime, or any crime if the person has a prior felony conviction.
The notice is required only when officers cannot confirm the person is lawfully in the United States.
The requirement would be written into the state constitution.
CO.yes: A yes vote requires law enforcement to notify federal immigration authorities in those cases.
CO.no: A no vote keeps current law, which has no such constitutional notification requirement.
CO.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff estimates about $60,000 in one-time state costs in FY 2026-27 for database access and computer updates, with no ongoing state cost and some added local workload.

CO.title: Constitutional Right to Purchase and Sell Natural Gas
CO.ballot_label: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution creating new law granting the right for consumers to purchase natural gas for cooking or heating in homes or businesses and for distributors and utilities to sell natural gas to consumers?
plain: Creates a constitutional right for consumers to buy natural gas for cooking or heating in homes and businesses.
Creates a matching right for distributors and utilities to sell natural gas for those uses.
Local building codes that restrict natural gas would have to be changed to fit the new right.
CO.yes: A yes vote adds a right to buy and sell natural gas for cooking and heating to the state constitution.
CO.no: A no vote leaves the constitution unchanged, so state and local governments keep their current authority over natural gas use.
CO.fiscal: No direct state revenue or spending change is estimated; state agency workload may rise and local governments with gas-restricting building codes would face costs to conform them.

CO.title: Constitutional Right to Hunt and Fish
CO.ballot_label: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution creating a constitutional right to hunt, fish, and harvest fish and wildlife by traditional methods, including all species of fish and wildlife managed by the state except non-game species, endangered species, or any species that is illegal to hunt under federal law, ...
plain: Adds a right to hunt, fish, and harvest wildlife by traditional methods to the state constitution.
Does not cover non-game species, endangered species, or species that are illegal to hunt under federal law.
Makes hunting and fishing the preferred way to manage wildlife, while the state keeps its power to regulate for conservation and public safety.
CO.yes: A yes vote creates a constitutional right to hunt and fish in Colorado.
CO.no: A no vote leaves hunting and fishing governed by current statutes and regulations without a constitutional right.
CO.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff expects no change to near-term state revenue or spending.

CO.title: Mail Ballot Voter Identification
CO.ballot_label: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution requiring a voter to sign and include the last four digits of their social security number or their Colorado driver's license or identification card number on the outside of their mail ballot for any federal or state election, ...
plain: Mail voters would have to sign and write the last four digits of their Social Security number, or their Colorado driver's license or ID number, on the outside of the ballot envelope.
Voters could fix missing or wrong information, including with other forms of ID.
County clerks could not count a mail ballot until the problem is fixed.
CO.yes: A yes vote adds an ID-number requirement for mail ballots in federal and state elections.
CO.no: A no vote keeps the current signature-and-affirmation process for mail ballots.
CO.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff estimates Department of State costs of $1.2 million in FY 2026-27, $260,000 in FY 2027-28, and $555,500 in FY 2028-29, plus county costs up to $2.5 million in 2026-27 (about 45% reimbursed by the state).

CO.title: Plain Language Ballot Titles
CO.ballot_label: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution concerning ballot question language, and, in connection therewith, requiring all state and local ballot questions to be written in plain language and at no more than an 8th grade reading level and prohibiting a state statute from requiring language that conflicts with these requirements in ballot questions for citizen-initiated measures?
plain: All state and local ballot questions would have to be written in plain language at no higher than an 8th-grade reading level.
State laws could not require wording in citizen-initiated ballot questions that conflicts with this rule.
The Title Board would set the standards for plain language and reading level.
CO.yes: A yes vote requires plain-language, 8th-grade-level ballot questions statewide.
CO.no: A no vote keeps current rules for how ballot questions are written.
CO.fiscal: No change in state revenue or spending; the Title Board may see minimal added workload.

CO.title: Requirements for Off-Cycle Congressional Redistricting
CO.ballot_label: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution concerning congressional redistricting, and, in connection therewith, reenacting the current process for congressional redistricting in the Colorado Constitution and prohibiting modifications to a final map unless at least three public meetings are held, ...
plain: Re-enacts Colorado's current independent commission process for drawing congressional districts.
Blocks changes to a final map unless at least three public meetings are held and the changes do not split communities of interest or purposely favor one party.
Any mid-decade map change would need approval from both the redistricting commission and the Colorado Supreme Court.
CO.yes: A yes vote requires commission and Supreme Court approval and public meetings before any off-cycle change to congressional maps.
CO.no: A no vote keeps the current process, which reviews maps only after each ten-year census.
CO.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff estimates about $370,000 in state costs and 1.0 FTE only in a year when off-cycle redistricting occurs, and no cost otherwise.

CO.title: Graduated Income Tax
CO.ballot_label: Shall state taxes be increased $2.7 billion annually, in order to increase or improve levels of public services, including K-12 public school education, health care, and early child care and education services, by an amendment to the Colorado Constitution and a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes ...
plain: Replaces Colorado's flat 4.4% income tax with graduated rates that rise with income, and removes the constitution's single-rate rule in TABOR.
The 4.4% rate stays for income from selling a primary home.
New revenue goes to the Colorado Future's Account for K-12 schools, health care, and early child care; the state may keep and spend it without TABOR refunds.
CO.yes: A yes vote creates a graduated income tax and dedicates the added revenue to education, health care, and child care.
CO.no: A no vote keeps the flat 4.4% income tax.
CO.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff estimates state revenue rises $958.4 million in FY 2026-27 (half year) and $1,972.0 million in FY 2027-28; taxpayers with taxable income under $510,834 pay less on average (about $176) and those above pay more.

CO.title: Keep and Spend Money for Education and Other Purposes
CO.ballot_label: Shall state investment in K-12 public education increase two percent each year for the next ten years, with investments used to increase teacher pay, improve teacher retention, lower class sizes, and increase access to career and technical courses, without raising taxes but instead funded by raising the annual limit on state fiscal year spending ...
plain: Raises the TABOR spending limit by the amount the state spends on K-12 education, so the state keeps money that would otherwise be refunded.
State K-12 funding would grow 2% a year for ten years, for teacher pay, teacher retention, smaller classes, and career and technical courses.
Requires a public, independent annual audit of how the money is spent; no tax rates change.
CO.yes: A yes vote lets the state keep and spend money above the TABOR cap for K-12 education instead of refunding it.
CO.no: A no vote keeps the current TABOR limit and refunds.
CO.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff estimates state spending rises $329.9 million in FY 2026-27 and $521.0 million in FY 2027-28, with TABOR refunds reduced by the same amounts.

CO.title: Increase Penalties for Fentanyl Crimes
CO.ballot_label: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes concerning criminal penalties for fentanyl and certain synthetic opioids, and, in connection therewith, increasing the felony classifications of drug-related crimes for distribution, manufacturing, dispensing, sale, or possession of fentanyl and certain synthetic opioids; creating mandated treatment for certain drug felony violations based on possession amount; ...
plain: Raises the felony level for making, selling, distributing, or possessing fentanyl and certain synthetic opioids.
Requires treatment for some drug felonies, depending on the amount possessed.
Narrows or removes sentencing exceptions for fentanyl crimes and drug-related deaths.
CO.yes: A yes vote increases penalties and adds mandated treatment for fentanyl-related crimes.
CO.no: A no vote keeps current fentanyl penalties and sentencing rules.
CO.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff estimates state spending of $876,488 in FY 2026-27, $8.9 million in FY 2027-28, and $24.8 million in FY 2028-29, mostly for prisons and courts, with mixed effects on local governments.

CO.title: Penalties for Human Trafficking of a Minor
CO.ballot_label: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes modifying existing law concerning human trafficking of a minor for sexual servitude, and, in connection therewith, creating new law expanding human trafficking of a minor for sexual servitude to include knowingly trading anything of monetary value to buy or sell sexual activity with a minor ...
plain: Makes human trafficking of a minor for sexual servitude a class 1 felony, punishable by life in prison without parole or release.
Expands the crime to include knowingly trading anything of value to buy or sell sexual activity with a minor.
Applies to offenses committed on or after January 1, 2027.
CO.yes: A yes vote requires life in prison without parole for trafficking a minor for sexual servitude.
CO.no: A no vote keeps the crime a class 2 felony with the current 8-to-24-year sentence range.
CO.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff expects no state cost until about FY 2041-42, when prison costs rise by roughly $180,000, growing to $360,000 a year, with minimal local impact.

CO.title: Male and Female Participation in School and Collegiate Sports
CO.ballot_label: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes creating new law restricting participation in all K-12 and collegiate school sports based on the participant's sex as determined by certain aspects of their biological reproductive system, and, in connection therewith, requiring a school, institution of higher education, or athletic association ...
plain: Every K-12 and college team or sport must be labeled male, female, or coed, and students may play only on the team matching their sex as defined by biological reproductive system, or on a coed team.
A female may join a male team if no female team exists.
Bars agencies and athletic associations from punishing schools for keeping separate female teams; the education commissioner enforces it for K-12.
CO.yes: A yes vote requires school and college sports teams to be separated by sex as defined in the measure.
CO.no: A no vote keeps current rules on team participation.
CO.fiscal: No state revenue or spending change is estimated; the Department of Education and school districts may see minimal workload and policy-update costs.

CO.title: Prohibit Surgery on Minors in Response to Perception of Sex or Gender
CO.ballot_label: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes modifying existing law by prohibiting surgery on a minor for the purpose of altering the minor's biological sex characteristics, and, in connection therewith, prohibiting any health-care professional or other person from knowingly performing, prescribing, administering, or providing any surgery to a minor ...
plain: Bans health-care professionals and others from performing or providing surgery on anyone under 18 to alter the minor's biological sex characteristics.
Bans using state or federal funds, Medicaid, or insurance coverage to pay for such surgery.
Takes effect January 1, 2027.
CO.yes: A yes vote prohibits sex-altering surgery on minors and public or insurance payment for it.
CO.no: A no vote keeps current law, which does not prohibit these surgeries.
CO.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff expects minimal fiscal impact, with possible small savings in Medicaid and state employee insurance and minimal added workload for regulators and courts.

CO.title: Income Tax Rate Limit
CO.ballot_label: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes capping the state income tax rate at 4.4% of federal taxable income for individuals and corporations?
plain: Makes the current 4.4% income tax rate the maximum rate for individuals and corporations, starting in tax year 2027.
Does not change the rate anyone pays today.
Conflicts with Amendment 87; if both pass, the one with more votes controls where they conflict.
CO.yes: A yes vote caps Colorado's income tax rate at 4.4% in state law.
CO.no: A no vote leaves the legislature and voters free to set the rate above 4.4% in the future.
CO.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff assesses the measure as having no fiscal impact because it keeps the existing 4.4% rate.

CO.title: Direct Sporting Goods Sales Tax Revenue for Conservation
CO.ballot_label: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes creating new law to increase water and land conservation funding without raising taxes, and, in connection therewith, through a voter-approved revenue change, allowing the state to keep and spend a portion of revenue from the state sales tax on sporting goods and equipment ...
plain: Lets the state keep and spend sales tax revenue from sporting goods and equipment instead of refunding it under TABOR.
The money would go to water, land, and forest conservation, wildfire prevention, and outdoor recreation.
Spending could be reduced if needed to protect funding for certain tax credits; no tax rates change.
CO.yes: A yes vote directs sporting-goods sales tax revenue to conservation and wildfire prevention without a TABOR refund.
CO.no: A no vote leaves that revenue subject to current TABOR refund rules.
CO.fiscal: Legislative Council Staff estimates about $175.0 million in FY 2027-28 and $180.2 million in FY 2028-29 redirected to conservation, reducing TABOR refunds by $175.0 million in FY 2027-28, with state spending rising to $54.9 million and then $131.8 million (excluding GOCO).

ID.title: Grant Legislature Exclusive Authority and Prohibit Citizen-Initiated Measures on Marijuana, Narcotics, and Psychoactive Substances Amendment
ID.ballot_label: Shall Section 26, Article III of the Constitution of the State of Idaho be amended to provide that only the Idaho Legislature shall have power and authority to legalize the growing, producing, manufacturing, transporting, selling, delivering, dispensing, administering, prescribing, distributing, possessing, or using of marijuana, narcotics, or other psychoactive substances?
plain: Only the Idaho Legislature could legalize marijuana, narcotics, or other psychoactive substances.
Citizens could no longer use the ballot initiative process to legalize these substances.
The amendment does not change any current statute on its own.
ID.yes: A yes vote gives the Legislature sole power to legalize marijuana, narcotics, or other psychoactive substances.
ID.no: A no vote keeps citizens' ability to propose initiatives that would legalize or decriminalize these substances.
ID.fiscal: The official fiscal note says there is no fiscal impact except the cost of placing the measure on the ballot, which the Secretary of State estimates at no more than $200,000.

ID.title: English as Official State Language Amendment
ID.ballot_label: Shall Article X of the Constitution of the State of Idaho be amended by the addition of a new Section 8, to provide that the English language shall be the official language for the state of Idaho, and to further provide that, except as required by federal law, English shall be used in all public proceedings, public documents, ...
plain: Makes English the official language of Idaho in the state constitution (it is already the official language in statute).
Requires English in public proceedings, public documents, public instruction, and other public acts of public institutions.
Exceptions apply where federal law requires another language.
ID.yes: A yes vote adds English as the official state language to the Idaho Constitution.
ID.no: A no vote leaves English as the official language in statute only.
ID.fiscal: The official fiscal note estimates up to $300,000 for the Secretary of State to publish the voter pamphlet, a cost that occurs anyway when other measures qualify for the ballot.

ID.title: Official State Gun Advisory Question
ID.ballot_label: Which of the following guns should be designated as the state gun of Idaho? Please choose only one answer. (a) Winchester Model 1894 (.30-30); (b) Winchester Model 1873 "Gun that Won the West" (.44-40); (c) 1873 Colt Single Action Army Revolver "Peacemaker" (.45 Colt); (d) M1 Garand rifle (.30-06); ...
plain: Asks voters which of six firearms they would like as Idaho's official state gun.
It is a non-binding advisory question; the Legislature would still have to pass a law to designate a state gun.
Voters choose only one option: (a) through (f).
ID.yes: There is no yes/no choice; voters pick one of six listed guns as their preference.
ID.no: Voters may leave the question blank; the result is advisory and does not change any law.
ID.fiscal: No fiscal note is shown; the question is advisory and non-binding.

ID.title: Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act
ID.ballot_label: Measure creating right to abortion before fetus viability, and post-viability to protect health; right to privacy; healthcare provider liability protections.
plain: Creates a legal right to abortion before fetal viability, and after viability in a medical emergency that threatens the woman's life or health.
Adds a right to reproductive freedom and privacy covering decisions such as contraception, fertility treatment, miscarriage care, and prenatal and postpartum care.
Protects patients, health-care providers, and those who assist them from penalties, and requires any restriction to be justified by a compelling state interest tied to the patient's health.
ID.yes: A yes vote creates a statutory right to abortion before viability (and after in medical emergencies) with provider liability protections.
ID.no: A no vote keeps Idaho's current law, which bans abortion except to prevent the woman's death or in the first trimester for reported rape or incest.
ID.fiscal: The state estimates the initiative would increase state spending by $3,100 to $7,800 a year (under 0.001% of the state share of Medicaid) for treating complications from chemical abortions.

HI.title: Increase Time for Senate to Act on Judicial Appointments Amendment
HI.ballot_label: Shall the Constitution of the State of Hawaii be amended to allow the Senate more time to consider and act on the appointments of justices and judges, by increasing the timeframe from thirty days to sixty days for appointments made between April 1 and December 31 when the Senate is not in regular session or is about to adjourn the regular session?
plain: The state Senate must confirm or reject the governor's and chief justice's judicial appointments within a set time.
This would extend that time from 30 days to 60 days for appointments made April 1 through December 31.
The longer window applies only when the Senate is not in regular session or is about to adjourn.
HI.yes: A yes vote gives the Senate up to 60 days (instead of 30) to act on judicial appointments made outside the regular session.
HI.no: A no vote keeps the current 30-day deadline for the Senate to act on judicial appointments.
HI.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate accompanies the ballot question.

HI.title: Resilient Infrastructure for Shelter and Equity (RISE) Bonds Amendment
HI.ballot_label: Shall the Hawaii State Constitution be amended to direct the legislature to authorize the counties to issue resilient infrastructure for shelter and equity bonds to fund public improvements in designated districts, repaid solely by future growth in property tax revenues within those districts, not by increasing real property tax rates, ...
plain: Lets the legislature authorize counties to issue "RISE" bonds to pay for public improvements in designated districts.
The bonds would be repaid only from future growth in property tax revenue in those districts, not from higher property tax rates.
These bonds would not count toward a county's debt limit and would be subject to accountability and oversight rules set by law.
HI.yes: A yes vote lets counties issue RISE bonds for infrastructure in designated districts, repaid from future property tax growth.
HI.no: A no vote leaves county bonding authority and debt limits as they are.
HI.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate accompanies the ballot question; the question states the bonds are repaid solely from future property tax growth in the districts, not by raising property tax rates.

WY.title: Homeowner's Primary Residence Property Tax Exemption
WY.ballot_label: PROPOSED INITIATIVE PROPOSITION NUMBER ONE Shall a law be enacted: Establishing a property tax exemption for qualified homeowners' primary residence in the amount of fifty percent (50%) of the assessed value of the dwelling; AND Defining "homeowner" and "primary residence"; providing that no more than one exemption shall apply to a single property ...
plain: Exempts 50% of the assessed value of a qualified homeowner's primary residence from property tax.

To qualify, a homeowner must have lived in Wyoming at least one year and occupied the home at least six months of the prior tax year, and file a sworn claim with the county assessor by the fourth Monday in May.
Only one exemption per property or owner each year; the exemption applies to the residential structure, and false claims carry a penalty.
WY.yes: A yes vote creates a 50% property tax exemption on a qualified homeowner's primary residence.
WY.no: A no vote keeps current property tax law with no new primary-residence exemption.
WY.fiscal: The ballot's official estimate projects property tax revenue decreases of $92,614,266 in fiscal year 2028 and $95,855,766 in fiscal year 2029, based on 2023 assessment data.

AL.title: Elections for Lieutenant Governor Vacancies and Legislative Authority Over Salaries Amendment
AL.ballot_label: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of Alabama of 2022, to provide for the election of a Lieutenant Governor if the Office of Lieutenant Governor becomes vacant during the first two years of a term, to authorize the Legislature to set the salary of the Lieutenant Governor and officers of the Legislature, and to require any expenditure of legislative funds for travel to be approved…
plain: If the lieutenant governor's office becomes empty during the first two years of a term, voters would elect a replacement.
The Legislature would be allowed to set the pay of the lieutenant governor and of its own officers.
Any use of legislative money for travel would need approval from a legislative officer.
AL.yes: A yes vote requires an election to fill a lieutenant governor vacancy that occurs more than 60 days before the next general election and lets the Legislature set the lieutenant governor's and legislative officers' salaries.
AL.no: A no vote keeps the current constitutional rules on lieutenant governor vacancies and salaries.
AL.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

AL.title: School District Consolidation Process Amendment
AL.ballot_label: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of Alabama of 2022, to provide a process for the creation of a consolidated county school system by merging two or more contiguous county boards of education; to require the State Board of Education to conduct an impact study on the potential effects of the consolidation; to require publication of the impact study;…
plain: Two or more neighboring county school boards could agree to merge into one multi-county school system.
Before a merger, the State Board of Education would have to study its effects and post the study online.
If 25 percent of voters in any affected district file a protest, the merger would need voter approval to go ahead.
AL.yes: A yes vote creates a constitutional process for neighboring county school boards to consolidate, with a required impact study and a protest-and-referendum step.
AL.no: A no vote leaves the constitution unchanged, with no such consolidation process.
AL.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

AL.title: Require the Pledge of Allegiance and Allow Student-Led Prayer in Public Schools Amendment
AL.ballot_label: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of Alabama of 2022, to require local boards of education to adopt policies requiring each public K-12 school to recite The Pledge of Allegiance to the United States flag at the beginning of each school day; and to require local boards of education to adopt a policy authorizing student-initiated and student-led prayer.
plain: Every public K-12 school would start each day by conducting the Pledge of Allegiance, and students could choose whether to say it.
Schools would also have to allow a prayer that is started and led by a student; no student could be required to take part.
Students could opt out of both the Pledge and the prayer based on their own beliefs.
AL.yes: A yes vote requires local school boards to adopt policies for a daily Pledge of Allegiance and for student-initiated, student-led prayer in public K-12 schools.
AL.no: A no vote leaves current law in place, with no constitutional requirement for these policies.
AL.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

AL.title: Broadcast The Star-Spangled Banner in Public Schools Amendment
AL.ballot_label: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of Alabama of 2022, to require local boards of education to adopt policies requiring each public K-12 school to broadcast or sanction the performance of the first stanza of The Star-Spangled Banner at least once per week during school hours.
plain: Each public K-12 school would have to broadcast the first verse of the national anthem at least once a week during school hours.
Schools would use a recording from the Library of Congress, or a school band, choir or singer could perform it instead.
Local school boards would write the policies to carry this out.
AL.yes: A yes vote requires public K-12 schools to broadcast or perform the first stanza of The Star-Spangled Banner at least weekly.
AL.no: A no vote does not add this requirement to the constitution.
AL.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

GA.title: Authorize Creation of Next Generation 9-1-1 Fund Amendment
GA.ballot_label: Shall the Constitution of Georgia be amended so as to authorize the General Assembly to dedicate certain existing revenues, including revenues reallocated by law, to a nonlapsing fund to be used exclusively for the expansion, maintenance, and operation of emergency 9-1-1 systems in this state?
plain: The Legislature could create a special fund called the Georgia Next Generation 9-1-1 Fund.
Money in the fund could only be spent to expand, maintain and run 9-1-1 systems, including upgrades to newer technology.
Money in the fund would not expire at the end of the year the way most state funds do.
GA.yes: A yes vote lets the General Assembly create and dedicate revenue to a nonlapsing fund used only for 9-1-1 systems.
GA.no: A no vote keeps the constitution as is, without authorizing a dedicated 9-1-1 fund.
GA.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

GA.title: Increase Acre Limit for Agriculture and Timber Conservation Use Property Tax Classification Amendment
GA.ballot_label: Shall the Constitution of Georgia, for the purpose of protecting family farmland, be amended so as to increase the maximum acreage to qualify for assessment and taxation as a bona fide conservation use property from 2,000 acres to 4,000 acres?
plain: Farm and timber land in the conservation-use program is taxed on its current use, which usually means a lower tax bill.
Today one owner can enroll up to 2,000 acres; this would raise the limit to 4,000 acres.
Owners must still promise to keep the land in conservation use for 10 years or pay back the tax savings.
GA.yes: A yes vote raises the per-owner cap for conservation use property tax treatment from 2,000 to 4,000 acres.
GA.no: A no vote keeps the cap at 2,000 acres.
GA.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

GA.title: Require Nonpartisan Elections for Probate Judges Amendment
GA.ballot_label: Shall the Constitution of Georgia be amended so as to require that all probate court judges be elected in nonpartisan elections?
plain: Probate judges handle wills, estates, guardianships and some licenses in each county.
Some probate judges now run with a party label; this would require all of them to run in nonpartisan elections.
Georgia's superior, state, appeals and Supreme Court judges are already elected without party labels.
GA.yes: A yes vote requires all probate judges to be elected on a nonpartisan basis.
GA.no: A no vote keeps allowing probate judges to be elected in partisan elections.
GA.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

NC.number: Constitutional Amendment (no number on ballot) – Voter ID
NC.title: Require Voter Identification Amendment
NC.ballot_label: Constitutional amendment to require all voters, not just those presenting to vote in person, to present photo identification before voting.
plain: North Carolina already requires photo ID for people who vote in person.
This would extend the photo ID requirement to all voters, including those who vote by mail.
The Legislature would set the rules for which IDs count and any exceptions.
NC.yes: A yes vote requires photo identification for all voters, including absentee-by-mail voters.
NC.no: A no vote keeps the photo ID requirement limited to in-person voting.
NC.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

NC.number: Constitutional Amendment (no number on ballot) – Income tax cap
NC.title: Reduce Income Tax Rate Cap from 7% to 3.5% Amendment
NC.ballot_label: Constitutional amendment to keep the State income tax rate from being raised higher than three and one-half percent (3.5%).
plain: The state constitution now caps the income tax rate at 7 percent.
This would lower that cap to 3.5 percent.
Lawmakers could not raise the income tax rate above 3.5 percent without another constitutional amendment.
NC.yes: A yes vote lowers the constitutional maximum income tax rate from 7% to 3.5%.
NC.no: A no vote keeps the maximum at 7%.
NC.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

NC.number: Constitutional Amendment (no number on ballot) – Property tax limits
NC.title: Property Tax Levy Limit Amendment
NC.ballot_label: Constitutional amendment requiring limits on property tax increases by local governments.
plain: Counties, cities and other local governments collect property taxes.
This would require the Legislature to pass laws limiting how much those property tax collections can increase.
The laws could include exceptions.
NC.yes: A yes vote requires the General Assembly to enact laws limiting increases in local property tax levies.
NC.no: A no vote does not add that requirement to the constitution.
NC.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

OK.title: Changes to Judicial Nominating Commission Amendment
OK.ballot_label: This measure amends article 7-B, section 3 of the Oklahoma Constitution, changing the Judicial Nominating Commission's structure. Currently appointments are based on congressional districts as constituted in 1967. If approved, appointments to the fifteen-member Commission will be as follows: 1) Governor appoints six members, including one from each congressional district as of the time of their appointment;…
plain: The Judicial Nominating Commission picks the finalists the governor chooses from when filling judge vacancies.
Its 15 members would be chosen by today's congressional districts instead of the 1967 map, and could serve two terms in a row.
Limits on how many members can come from one political party, and on lawyers or their relatives serving, would be removed.
OK.yes: A yes vote changes the commission's appointment districts, terms, party-balance rule and eligibility rules as described.
OK.no: A no vote keeps the commission's current structure.
OK.fiscal: The official ballot title states the measure will not have a fiscal impact.

OK.title: Reduce Annual Increases in Property Values for Tax Calculations Amendment
OK.ballot_label: This measure amends article 10, sections 8B and 8C of the Oklahoma Constitution. Currently, section 8B limits annual growth in fair cash value to 5% for most real property or 3% for homesteads and agricultural land. If approved, the measure would limit annual growth in fair cash value for tax year 2027 and after to 4% for most real property…
plain: Starting in 2027, the taxable value of most property could rise no more than 4% a year (down from 5%), and homes and farmland no more than 1.75% (down from 3%).
The senior freeze for homeowners 65 and older would no longer have an income cap, but values could rise up to 1.75% a year depending on household income.
Seniors with household income at or below their area's median would still see no increase in value.
OK.yes: A yes vote lowers the annual caps on growth in assessed property values and reworks the senior freeze as described.
OK.no: A no vote keeps the current 5% and 3% caps and the existing senior freeze rules.
OK.fiscal: The official ballot title states the measure would have a fiscal impact on the state, but the exact impact is unknown.

AR.title: The Citizens Only Voting Amendment (Citizenship Voting Requirement Amendment)
AR.ballot_label: An amendment to the Arkansas Constitution to create "The Citizens Only Voting Amendment"; to provide that only a citizen of the United States meeting the qualifications of an elector under the Arkansas Constitution may vote in an election in this state; and providing that a person who does not meet the qualifications of an elector under the Arkansas Constitution shall not…
plain: The Arkansas Constitution already says voters must be U.S. citizens, state residents, at least 18 and registered.
This adds that only a U.S. citizen who meets those requirements may vote in any election in the state.
It also says anyone who does not meet the requirements cannot vote in any state or local election.
AR.yes: A yes vote adds language that only U.S. citizens meeting elector qualifications may vote in any state or local election.
AR.no: A no vote leaves the current voter-qualification language unchanged.
AR.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

AR.title: Right to Keep and Bear Arms Amendment
AR.ballot_label: An amendment to the Arkansas Constitution to provide that the citizens of the State of Arkansas shall have the right to keep and bear arms for their common defense, for lawful hunting and recreational use, and for any other lawful purpose; providing that the right to keep and bear arms includes without limitation the possession and use of ammunition,…
plain: The constitution now protects the right to keep and bear arms for the people's common defense.
This would add lawful hunting, recreation and any other lawful purpose, and would cover ammunition, accessories and gun parts.
It would declare the right natural, fundamental and individual, and say it shall not be infringed.
AR.yes: A yes vote expands the constitutional right to keep and bear arms as described, including ammunition, accessories and components.
AR.no: A no vote keeps the current wording, which protects the right to keep and bear arms for the common defense.
AR.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

AR.title: Creation of Economic Development Districts Amendment
AR.ballot_label: An amendment to the Arkansas Constitution concerning economic development in the State of Arkansas; and authorizing the General Assembly to provide for the creation of economic development districts within cities, counties, or cooperative areas to promote economic development within the economic development district.
plain: The Legislature could create programs and give loans or grants of public money to grow the economy, reduce unemployment, expand transportation and commerce, or develop real estate.
It could also allow cities, counties or groups of them to create economic development districts.
Those districts could issue bonds for projects, and the bonds would not count toward some existing constitutional debt limits.
AR.yes: A yes vote lets the General Assembly create economic development programs, loans, grants and economic development districts that can issue bonds.
AR.no: A no vote keeps the current constitutional limits on public loans, grants and local debt.
AR.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

AR.title: Arkansas Water, Waste Disposal, and Pollution Abatement Facilities Financing Act of 2025 (Natural Resources Commission Bond Measure)
AR.ballot_label: Popular name: Arkansas Water, Waste Disposal, and Pollution Abatement Facilities Financing Act of 2025 (referred state statute authorizing up to $500 million in general obligation bonds).
plain: The state could borrow up to $500 million by selling bonds for water, waste disposal, pollution control, drainage, irrigation and flood control projects.
No more than $60 million could be issued in any two-year period without added legislative approval, and no more than $165 million could go to irrigation.
The bonds would be repaid over up to 35 years from state general revenue and loan repayments from the projects.
AR.yes: A yes vote authorizes the Arkansas Natural Resources Commission to issue up to $500 million in general obligation bonds for water-related infrastructure.
AR.no: A no vote does not authorize the new bonded debt.
AR.fiscal: Authorizes up to $500 million in general obligation bonds, repaid over up to 35 years from state general revenue and project loan repayments (per the UA Cooperative Extension voter guide); no separate official fiscal estimate was located.

KY.title: Limit Governor's Pardon Power and Commutations Near General Election Amendment (Senate Bill 10)
KY.ballot_label: Are you in favor of limiting a Governor's ability to grant pardons or commute sentences by prohibiting him or her from granting pardons or commuting sentences during the time period beginning 60 days prior to the general election at which the Governor is elected, and ending when the Governor is sworn in for that term…
plain: Kentucky's governor can now grant pardons and shorten sentences at any time.
This would block the governor from granting pardons or commuting sentences from 60 days before the governor's election until the new term begins (the fifth Tuesday after the election).
The governor would still have to file a public statement of reasons for each pardon decision.
KY.yes: A yes vote bars the governor from issuing pardons or commutations during the window from 60 days before the gubernatorial election until the new term starts.
KY.no: A no vote keeps the governor's current unrestricted timing for pardons and commutations.
KY.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

TN.title: Remove Right to Bail for Certain Criminal Offenses Amendment
TN.ballot_label: Official summary: This amendment changes Article I, section 15 of the Tennessee Constitution by allowing a court to hold a defendant without bail before trial when that defendant is accused of: an offense punishable by the death penalty, an act of terrorism, second degree murder, aggravated rape of a child, aggravated rape, grave torture, or any crime for which a convicted person…
plain: Today judges must allow bail for everyone except in death-penalty cases where the evidence is strong.

This would let judges deny bail before trial for people accused of terrorism, second-degree murder, aggravated rape, aggravated rape of a child, grave torture, or crimes requiring 85% of the sentence to be served, when the evidence is strong.
Judges would have to state on the record why they granted or denied bail in those cases.
TN.yes: A yes vote lets courts deny pretrial bail for the listed serious offenses when the proof is evident or presumption great.
TN.no: A no vote keeps bail available in all cases except capital offenses.
TN.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

TN.title: Prohibit State Property Taxes Amendment
TN.ballot_label: Official summary: This amendment adds text to Article II, section 28 of the Tennessee Constitution that prohibits the Legislature from imposing a State property tax on real, personal, or mixed property.
plain: Tennessee has no statewide property tax today; local governments collect property taxes.
This would write a ban on any state-level property tax into the constitution.
Local property taxes would not be affected.
TN.yes: A yes vote prohibits the Legislature from ever levying a state property tax.
TN.no: A no vote leaves the Legislature's existing authority over property taxation unchanged.
TN.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

TN.title: Marsy's Law Crime Victims' Rights Amendment
TN.ballot_label: Official summary: This amendment changes Article I, section 35 of the Tennessee Constitution by clarifying existing rights for crime victims and adding new rights. The amendment gives victims new rights: to fair treatment; to be informed about and participate in the parole process; to be protected from harassment, intimidation, and abuse; to be informed of the minimum sentence the convicted criminal will…
plain: The constitution already lists some rights for crime victims; this replaces that list with a longer one, often called Marsy's Law.
New rights include fair treatment, taking part in parole hearings, protection from harassment, and knowing the offender's minimum sentence and release date.
It does not limit prosecutors or courts and does not let victims sue the state for money.
TN.yes: A yes vote replaces the current victims' rights section with the expanded list of rights.
TN.no: A no vote keeps the existing list of crime victims' rights.
TN.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

MD.title: Arbitration Reform for State Employees Act of 2026 (Constitutional Amendment, Ch. 155 of the 2026 Legislative Session)
MD.ballot_label: Providing that each budget submitted by the Governor shall include proposed expenditures necessary to implement wages, hours, fringe benefits, health benefits, and other terms and conditions of employment in each collective bargaining memorandum of understanding with State employees, whether the State and State employees reached those terms and conditions by mutual agreement or through a neutral decider's order.
plain: State employee unions and the state sign agreements on pay, hours and benefits.
This would require the governor's yearly budget to include enough money to pay for what those agreements say.
It applies whether the terms were negotiated or set by a neutral arbitrator.
MD.yes: A yes vote means the Governor must include money in the proposed State budget to pay for agreements between the State and its employees, whether negotiated or decided by a neutral decision-maker.
MD.no: A no vote means the law about funding agreements between the State and State employees stays the same.
MD.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

MD.title: Temporary Appointments on the Commission on Judicial Disabilities (Constitutional Amendment, Ch. 878 of the 2026 Legislative Session)
MD.ballot_label: Authorizing temporary substitute appointments to the Commission on Judicial Disabilities when a member is recused or disqualified, or when a member's term expires. In these situations, the Commission Chair may recall a former member of the Commission, or the Governor, at the request of the Commission Chair, may appoint a temporary substitute member or extend the term of a current member…
plain: The Commission on Judicial Disabilities reviews complaints about judges.
If a member steps aside, is disqualified, or a term ends with no replacement, the chair could bring back a former member to fill in temporarily.
The governor, at the chair's request, could also name a temporary substitute or extend a current member's term until a permanent replacement is appointed.
MD.yes: A yes vote allows temporary appointments to the Commission when a member is recused, disqualified, or a term ends without a replacement.
MD.no: A no vote keeps the current membership rules, with no temporary appointments allowed.
MD.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

MD.title: Election Districts (Constitutional Amendment, Ch. 881 of the 2026 Legislative Session)
MD.ballot_label: FOR the purpose of clarifying that certain requirements apply only to districts for the election of members of the Senate of Maryland and the House of Delegates; authorizing the General Assembly to grant original jurisdiction to the Supreme Court of Maryland to review the congressional districting plan of the State; and providing that nothing in the Maryland Constitution provides applicable criteria…
plain: The constitution requires state legislative districts to be compact, connected and roughly equal in population; this says those rules apply only to state legislative districts, not congressional districts.
It states that nothing in the Maryland Constitution sets criteria for congressional district lines.
The General Assembly could let the Supreme Court of Maryland hear challenges to a congressional map directly.
MD.yes: A yes vote limits the constitutional districting criteria to state legislative districts and declares the constitution sets no criteria for congressional districts.
MD.no: A no vote leaves the constitution's districting language as it is.
MD.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

NH.title: Eliminate Office of Register of Probate Amendment
NH.ballot_label: Are you in favor of eliminating the office of register of probate by amending articles 71 and 81 of the second part of the constitution to read as follows:… (full text of Articles 71 and 81 as amended follows on the ballot)
plain: The constitution now lists the register of probate among the county officers that voters elect.
This would remove the register of probate from that list, eliminating the office.
It would also remove the reference to registers of probate in the rule that bars judges from acting as lawyers in probate cases.
NH.yes: A yes vote removes the office of register of probate from the New Hampshire Constitution; a two-thirds vote is needed to pass.
NH.no: A no vote keeps the office of register of probate in the constitution.
NH.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published.

MT.title: Keep judicial elections nonpartisan
MT.ballot_label: CI-132 amends the Montana Constitution to require that judicial elections remain nonpartisan. [] YES on Constitutional Amendment CI-132 [] NO on Constitutional Amendment CI-132
plain: CI-132 would add a new section to the Montana Constitution saying that judicial elections shall remain nonpartisan.
Under Montana law today, candidates for judge already run without a political party label next to their names.
Putting the rule in the constitution means the Legislature could not change it by passing an ordinary law.
MT.yes: A yes vote adds a new Section 12 to Article VII of the Montana Constitution providing that judicial elections shall remain nonpartisan.
MT.no: A no vote leaves the Montana Constitution unchanged, so the nonpartisan format of judicial elections continues to rest on state statute rather than the constitution.
MT.fiscal: No fiscal statement is printed on the official ballot language issued by the Montana Secretary of State for CI-132, and the 2026 Montana Voter Information Pamphlet had not been published as of Sept 22, 2026. No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept 22, 2026.

MT.title: Right to use the initiative and referendum process
MT.ballot_label: The Montana constitution reserves to the people the powers of initiative and referendum. CI-133 amends the constitution to secure this fundamental right from interference by the government. Specifically, CI-133 requires impartial, predictable, open, and timely processes for ballot issues. Petitions and ballot statements must be approved within 90 days of the initial submission, and legal challenges to ballot qualification must be resolved before the deadline for finalizing ballots. CI-133 requires the state to allow ample time for signature gathering, prohibits disqualification of petitions because of minor or technical issues, allows voters to withdraw their signatures if they so choose, and prohibits the use of government resources to support or oppose a ballot measure. [] YES on Constitutional Amendment CI-133 [] NO on Constitutional Amendment CI-133
plain: CI-133 would add a new section to the Montana Constitution stating that people have a fundamental right to use the initiative and referendum process.
It would require the state to approve petitions and ballot statements within 90 days of the first submission and to resolve court challenges before ballots are finalized.
It would also bar rejecting petitions over minor or technical errors, let voters withdraw their own signatures, and prohibit using government resources to support or oppose a ballot measure.
MT.yes: A yes vote adds a new Section 37 to Article II of the Montana Constitution establishing a fundamental right to initiative and referendum and the procedural guarantees listed in the measure.
MT.no: A no vote leaves the Montana Constitution unchanged, so the rules for qualifying and challenging ballot issues continue to be set by statute.
MT.fiscal: No fiscal statement is printed on the official ballot language issued by the Montana Secretary of State for CI-133, and the 2026 Montana Voter Information Pamphlet had not been published as of Sept 22, 2026. No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept 22, 2026.

MT.title: Limit election spending by corporations and similar entities
MT.ballot_label: I-194, if passed, limits the powers of artificial persons to those powers necessary or convenient as provided by law. These powers must exclude contributing anything of value to candidate elections, supporting or opposing political parties, or supporting or opposing state or local ballot issues. Artificial persons include non-profits, trusts, partnerships, corporations, trade associations, or unincorporated associations and includes all such entities doing business in Montana. Any violation of I-194 is punished by forfeiting all privileges to do business in Montana. Those privileges may be, but are not automatically, restored upon disgorgement and certification of compliance with I-194. I-194 does not apply to the distribution of news, commentary, or editorial content. I-194 also does not apply to the state of Montana, political subdivisions, individuals, political committees, or public corporations. [] YES on Initiative I-194 [] NO on Initiative I-194
plain: I-194 would change state law so that corporations, nonprofits, trusts, partnerships, trade associations, and similar entities do not have the legal power to spend money on Montana elections.
An entity that spends money to support or oppose a candidate, a political party, or a ballot issue would forfeit its Montana charter privileges, including limited liability.
The law would not apply to individuals, political committees, state or local government bodies, or to publishing news, commentary, and editorial content.
MT.yes: A yes vote enacts a new chapter of Montana statute, effective January 1, 2027, that withholds political spending power from artificial persons and makes such spending void and grounds for forfeiture of charter privileges.
MT.no: A no vote leaves Montana statute unchanged, so existing law governing political spending by corporations and other entities continues to apply.
MT.fiscal: No fiscal statement is printed on the official ballot language issued by the Montana Secretary of State for I-194, and the 2026 Montana Voter Information Pamphlet had not been published as of Sept 22, 2026. No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept 22, 2026.

NV.title: State Question No. 6 - Amendment to the Nevada Constitution, Initiative Petition C-05-2023
NV.ballot_label: Should the Nevada Constitution be amended to create an individual's fundamental right to an abortion, without interference by state or local governments, whenever the abortion is performed by a qualified healthcare professional until fetal viability or when necessary to protect the health or life of the pregnant individual at any point during the pregnancy? Yes [ ] No [ ]
plain: Question 6 would add a new section to the Nevada Constitution creating a fundamental right to an abortion performed by a qualified health care professional.
That right would apply until fetal viability, and after that point when an abortion is needed to protect the life or health of the pregnant patient.

This is the second of two required votes: Nevada voters approved the same amendment in 2024, and an initiated constitutional amendment must pass at two general elections in a row before it becomes part of the constitution.
NV.yes: A yes vote gives the amendment the second of the two approvals it needs, adding a new Section 25 to Article 1 of the Nevada Constitution that establishes a constitutional right to abortion, effective when the vote is canvassed on November 24, 2026.
NV.no: A no vote rejects the amendment, so it does not become part of the Nevada Constitution and abortion remains legal in Nevada only as a matter of state statute.
NV.fiscal: Official fiscal note in the Secretary of State's 2026 guide: "FINANCIAL IMPACT - CANNOT BE DETERMINED." The Legislative Counsel Bureau's Fiscal Analysis Division found that if the amendment passes, the Legislature may have to review existing abortion laws for compliance, which could affect state or local resources; but because it is unknown which laws, if any, would be out of compliance or how the Legislature would revise them, the financial effect on state or local governments cannot be determined with any reasonable degree of certainty. Prepared by the Fiscal Analysis Division of the Legislative Counsel Bureau, August 1, 2024.

NV.title: State Question No. 7 - Amendment to the Nevada Constitution, Initiative Petition C-02-2023
NV.ballot_label: Should the Nevada Constitution be amended to require voters to either present photo identification to verify their identity when voting in-person or to provide certain personal information to verify their identity when voting by mail ballot? Yes [ ] No [ ]
plain: Question 7 would amend the Nevada Constitution to require voters to show a photo ID before receiving a ballot at a polling place.
Voters using a mail ballot would instead provide identifying numbers, such as the last four digits of a Nevada driver's license or Social Security number.

This is the second of two required votes: Nevada voters approved the same amendment in 2024, and an initiated constitutional amendment must pass at two general elections in a row before it becomes part of the constitution.
NV.yes: A yes vote gives the amendment the second of the two approvals it needs, adding new Sections 1B and 1C to Article 2 of the Nevada Constitution that require photo ID for in-person voting and identifying information for mail ballots, effective when the vote is canvassed on November 24, 2026.
NV.no: A no vote rejects the amendment, so it does not become part of the Nevada Constitution and current identification rules for voting continue to apply.
NV.fiscal: Official fiscal note in the Secretary of State's 2026 guide: "FINANCIAL IMPACT - YES." Based on information from the Secretary of State's Office, changes to Nevada's voter check-in and mail-ballot verification systems would cost approximately $6,750 and would have to be made in time for the 2028 elections. The Fiscal Analysis Division also assumes the Legislature would need to create a free alternative form of voter ID for people who lack an accepted document, and because the form, issuing agency, and number of affected voters are unknown, that additional financial effect on state or local governments cannot be determined with any reasonable degree of certainty. Prepared by the Fiscal Analysis Division of the Legislative Counsel Bureau, July 29, 2024.

NM.title: Constitutional Amendment 1 (House Joint Resolution 2, 2025 Regular Session - "Eliminate Pocket Vetoes, CA")
NM.ballot_label: Proposing an amendment to Article 4, Section 22 of the Constitution of New Mexico to require the governor to provide veto messages on all bills vetoed in whole or in part and to provide that all bills passed by the legislature and not acted on by the governor will become law.
plain: Constitutional Amendment 1 would require the governor to give a written veto message for every bill or part of a bill that is vetoed.
Bills the Legislature passes that the governor does not act on would become law instead of dying without any action.
This would end the practice in New Mexico known as the pocket veto.
NM.yes: A yes vote amends Article 4, Section 22 of the New Mexico Constitution to require veto messages for all vetoes and to make unsigned, unvetoed bills become law.
NM.no: A no vote leaves Article 4, Section 22 unchanged, so a bill the governor neither signs nor vetoes after the session ends continues to die without an explanation.
NM.fiscal: Legislative Finance Committee fiscal impact report on House Joint Resolution 2 (2025), "Eliminate Pocket Vetoes, CA": estimated Secretary of State cost of $30,000 to $50,000, nonrecurring, from other state funds, to place the amendment before voters; the impact on the Office of the Governor is listed as indeterminate but minimal.

NM.title: Constitutional Amendment 2 (Senate Joint Resolution 1, 2026 Regular Session - "School Election Timing, CA")
NM.ballot_label: Proposing to amend Article 7, Section 1 of the Constitution of New Mexico to remove the requirement that school elections be separate from partisan elections.
plain: Constitutional Amendment 2 would delete the constitutional rule that school elections must be held at a different time from partisan elections.
School districts could then put their races and bond questions on the same ballot as a general election.
The timing of school elections would instead be set by state law.
NM.yes: A yes vote amends Article 7, Section 1 of the New Mexico Constitution to strike the requirement that school elections be held at different times from partisan elections.
NM.no: A no vote leaves Article 7, Section 1 unchanged, so school elections must continue to be held separately from partisan elections.
NM.fiscal: Legislative Finance Committee fiscal impact report on Senate Joint Resolution 1 (2026), "School Election Timing, CA": election costs of $35,000 to $50,000, nonrecurring, from the general fund, to print and publish the amendment for voters; enactment costs are listed as no fiscal impact.

NM.title: Constitutional Amendment 3 (House Joint Resolution 1, 2026 Regular Session - "Boards of Regents Nominating Committees, CA")
NM.ballot_label: Proposing an amendment to Article 12, Section 13 of the Constitution of New Mexico to establish nominating committees to provide lists of nominees to the governor for appointment of nonstudent members to the boards of regents of state educational institutions; providing that student members of boards of regents shall be appointed from a list provided by an elected student governing body of the institution; providing that, except for a student member, members of the boards of regents shall not have changed their political party registration in the twelve months preceding appointment.
plain: Constitutional Amendment 3 would create nominating committees that give the governor a list of candidates for the boards of regents of state colleges and universities.
The governor would have to choose non-student regents from that list, and student regents from a list provided by an elected student government.
Except for student members, a person could not be appointed as a regent if they changed their political party registration in the previous twelve months.
NM.yes: A yes vote amends Article 12, Section 13 of the New Mexico Constitution to require nominating committees for regent appointments and to impose the party-registration and student-nomination conditions described in the measure.
NM.no: A no vote leaves Article 12, Section 13 unchanged, so the governor continues to nominate regents under the current process.
NM.fiscal: Legislative Finance Committee fiscal impact report on House Joint Resolution 1 (2026), "Boards of Regents Nominating Committees, CA": estimated Secretary of State cost of $35,000 to $50,000 in FY27, nonrecurring, from the general fund.

NM.title: Constitutional Amendment 4 (House Joint Resolution 5, 2026 Regular Session - "Legislative Compensation, CA")
NM.ballot_label: Proposing to amend Article 4, Section 10 of the Constitution of New Mexico to allow legislative compensation that is limited to the median household income for New Mexico, to require legislative compensation to be reduced if the median household income for New Mexico falls, to allow legislative compensation to be increased only if the median household income for New Mexico rises and to provide for delayed implementation.
plain: Constitutional Amendment 4 would allow New Mexico legislators to be paid a salary, which the constitution does not currently permit.
The salary could be no more than the state's median household income.
Legislative pay would rise only if the state's median household income rises and would be cut if it falls, and the change would take effect on a delayed schedule.
NM.yes: A yes vote amends Article 4, Section 10 of the New Mexico Constitution to permit legislative compensation capped at the state median household income, on the delayed schedule set out in the amendment.
NM.no: A no vote leaves Article 4, Section 10 unchanged, so New Mexico legislators continue to serve without a salary.
NM.fiscal: Legislative Finance Committee fiscal impact report on House Joint Resolution 5 (2026), "Legislative Compensation, CA": about $35,000 nonrecurring general fund for the Secretary of State to put the amendment before voters, and, if the amendment is ratified, about $3,800,000 in recurring general fund costs to the Legislative Council Service beginning in FY2028. The report notes the amounts do not include employer payroll taxes (10-12 percent of payroll) or benefits (up to 30 percent).

NM.title: Bond Question 1 - Senior Citizen Facility Improvement, Construction and Equipment Acquisition Bonds (2026 Capital Projects General Obligation Bond Act)
NM.ballot_label: The 2026 Capital Projects General Obligation Bond Act authorizes the issuance and sale of senior citizen facility improvement, construction and equipment acquisition bonds. Shall the state be authorized to issue general obligation bonds in an amount not to exceed twenty-one million five hundred eighty-two thousand two hundred thirteen dollars ($21,582,213) to make capital expenditures for certain senior citizen facility improvement, construction and equipment acquisition projects and provide for a general property tax imposition and levy for the payment of principal of, interest on and expenses incurred in connection with the issuance of the bonds and the collection of the tax as permitted by law?
plain: Bond Question 1 would let the state borrow up to $21,582,213 by issuing general obligation bonds.
The money would pay for building, improving, and equipping senior citizen facilities across New Mexico.
A general property tax would be imposed and collected to repay the bond principal, the interest, and the costs of issuing the bonds.
NM.yes: A yes vote authorizes the state to issue up to $21,582,213 in general obligation bonds for senior citizen facility projects and to levy a general property tax to repay them.
NM.no: A no vote denies the bond authorization, so the state may not issue these bonds or levy the associated property tax for these projects.
NM.fiscal: The official fiscal terms are stated in the ballot question itself: general obligation bonds in an amount not to exceed $21,582,213, repaid through a general property tax imposition and levy covering principal, interest, and issuance expenses. No separate dollar fiscal estimate beyond the ballot text was published by the Secretary of State as of Sept 22, 2026.

NM.title: Bond Question 2 - Library Acquisition Bonds (2026 Capital Projects General Obligation Bond Act)
NM.ballot_label: The 2026 Capital Projects General Obligation Bond Act authorizes the issuance and sale of library acquisition bonds. Shall the state be authorized to issue general obligation bonds in an amount not to exceed nineteen million three hundred twenty-four thousand one hundred eighty-eight dollars ($19,324,188) to make capital expenditures for academic, public school, public and tribal library resource acquisitions and provide for a general property tax imposition and levy for the payment of principal of, interest on and expenses incurred in connection with the issuance of the bonds and the collection of the tax as permitted by law?
plain: Bond Question 2 would let the state borrow up to $19,324,188 by issuing general obligation bonds.
The money would buy library resources for academic libraries, public school libraries, public libraries, and tribal libraries.
A general property tax would be imposed and collected to repay the bond principal, the interest, and the costs of issuing the bonds.
