NM.yes: A yes vote authorizes the state to issue up to $19,324,188 in general obligation bonds for library resource acquisitions and to levy a general property tax to repay them.
NM.no: A no vote denies the bond authorization, so the state may not issue these bonds or levy the associated property tax for these acquisitions.
NM.fiscal: The official fiscal terms are stated in the ballot question itself: general obligation bonds in an amount not to exceed $19,324,188, repaid through a general property tax imposition and levy covering principal, interest, and issuance expenses. No separate dollar fiscal estimate beyond the ballot text was published by the Secretary of State as of Sept 22, 2026.

NM.title: Bond Question 3 - Higher Education, Special Schools and Tribal Schools Capital Improvement and Acquisition Bonds (2026 Capital Projects General Obligation Bond Act)
NM.ballot_label: The 2026 Capital Projects General Obligation Bond Act authorizes the issuance and sale of higher education, special schools and tribal schools capital improvement and acquisition bonds. Shall the state be authorized to issue general obligation bonds in an amount not to exceed three hundred fifty-two million two hundred twenty five thousand three hundred seventy-nine dollars ($352,225,379) to make capital expenditures for certain higher education, special schools and tribal schools capital improvements and acquisitions and provide for a general property tax imposition and levy for the payment of principal of, interest on and expenses incurred in connection with the issuance of the bonds and the collection of the tax as permitted by law?
plain: Bond Question 3 would let the state borrow up to $352,225,379 by issuing general obligation bonds.
The money would pay for capital improvements and acquisitions at higher education institutions, special schools, and tribal schools.
A general property tax would be imposed and collected to repay the bond principal, the interest, and the costs of issuing the bonds.
NM.yes: A yes vote authorizes the state to issue up to $352,225,379 in general obligation bonds for higher education, special school, and tribal school capital projects and to levy a general property tax to repay them.
NM.no: A no vote denies the bond authorization, so the state may not issue these bonds or levy the associated property tax for these projects.
NM.fiscal: The official fiscal terms are stated in the ballot question itself: general obligation bonds in an amount not to exceed $352,225,379, repaid through a general property tax imposition and levy covering principal, interest, and issuance expenses. No separate dollar fiscal estimate beyond the ballot text was published by the Secretary of State as of Sept 22, 2026.

UT.title: Constitutional Amendment A (H.J.R. 10, 2025 General Session - Proposal to Amend Utah Constitution - Publication Amendments)
UT.ballot_label: Constitutional Amendment A. Shall the Utah Constitution be amended to change how proposed constitutional amendments are published, requiring publication for 60 days immediately before the general election in a manner established by state law instead of in newspapers? If voters approve Constitutional Amendment A, state statute would change to require the Lieutenant Governor to publish the full text of all proposed constitutional amendments and other ballot questions from the Legislature, on the Utah Public Notice Website and on the Lieutenant Governor's website for 60 days immediately before the general election. ( ) For ( ) Against
plain: Constitutional Amendment A would change how the state must publish proposed constitutional amendments before an election.
Instead of printing them in a newspaper in every county for two months, they would be published for the 60 days immediately before the general election in a manner set by state law.
State law would then require the lieutenant governor to post the full text on the Utah Public Notice Website and on the lieutenant governor's website.
UT.yes: A for vote amends Article XXIII, Section 1 of the Utah Constitution to replace the two-month newspaper publication requirement with 60 days of publication in a manner provided by statute, effective January 1, 2027.
UT.no: An against vote leaves Article XXIII, Section 1 unchanged, so proposed constitutional amendments must continue to be published in a newspaper in every county where one is published, for two months before the election.
UT.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept 22, 2026. Utah's 2026 Voter Information Pamphlet, which carries the Office of Legislative Research and General Counsel's impartial analysis and its identification of the measure's fiscal effects, had not been published as of that date.

UT.title: Constitutional Amendment B (S.J.R. 2, 2025 General Session - Proposal to Amend Utah Constitution - Statewide Initiatives)
UT.ballot_label: Constitutional Amendment B. Shall the Utah Constitution be amended to require that citizen-proposed laws that increase taxes compared to existing law be approved by at least 60% of voters, instead of a simple majority? ( ) For ( ) Against
plain: Constitutional Amendment B would raise the share of votes needed to pass a citizen initiative that increases taxes.
Such an initiative would need approval from at least 60% of those voting on it instead of a simple majority.
It applies to initiatives that create a new tax, extend an existing tax to more items or transactions, raise a tax rate, or reduce a property tax rate by less than current law would.
UT.yes: A for vote amends Article VI, Section 1 of the Utah Constitution so that initiated legislation voted on after November 1, 2026 that makes the listed tax changes must be approved by at least 60% of those voting, effective November 23, 2026.
UT.no: An against vote leaves Article VI, Section 1 unchanged, so citizen initiatives that raise taxes continue to pass with a simple majority.
UT.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept 22, 2026. Utah's 2026 Voter Information Pamphlet, which carries the Office of Legislative Research and General Counsel's impartial analysis and its identification of the measure's fiscal effects, had not been published as of that date.

WA.title: Initiative Measure No. IP26-645 - An Initiative Prohibiting Individual Income Taxes (Initiative to the People)
WA.ballot_label: Initiative Measure No. IP26-645 concerns state and local taxes. This measure would repeal a 9.9% tax on annual individual income over $1,000,000; prohibit taxes measured by individual income and taxes on individual income or the receipt of individual income; and define "income." This measure would decrease funding for public K-12 education, higher education (including universities and community colleges), and human services (primarily healthcare). Should this measure be enacted into law? Yes [ ] No [ ]
plain: Initiative IP26-645 would repeal the 9.9% state tax on individual income above $1,000,000 that the Legislature enacted in 2026 and that was set to begin in 2028.
It would also bar state and local governments from imposing taxes on individual income, on the receipt of individual income, or measured by individual income.
It would define "income" and "individual" for state excise tax purposes, while leaving in place the other tax credits, exemptions, and deductions enacted alongside the tax.
WA.yes: A yes vote enacts the measure, repealing the 9.9% tax on individual income over $1,000,000 and prohibiting state and local individual income taxes, effective December 3, 2026.
WA.no: A no vote rejects the measure, so the 9.9% tax on individual income over $1,000,000 takes effect as scheduled and no new prohibition on income taxes is added to state law.
WA.fiscal: Office of Financial Management fiscal impact statement: if approved, Initiative 645 will result in an estimated loss to state revenue of $11.4 billion over state fiscal years 2027-2031 (total revenue loss of $11,432,414,000 across the state general fund, federal general fund, and fair start for kids account). This would reduce funding to the state general fund for core government services, particularly public K-12 education, higher education, and human services (primarily healthcare). State agency savings are estimated at a net total of $150,471,700 over five state fiscal years. The measure is also subject to a public investment impact disclosure stating it "would decrease funding for public K-12 education, higher education (including universities and community colleges), and human services (primarily healthcare)."

WA.title: Initiative Measure No. IL26-001 - An Act Relating to the Washington Parents' Bill of Rights (Initiative to the Legislature)
WA.ballot_label: Initiative Measure No. IL26-001 concerns parental rights relating to their children in public school. This measure would repeal amendments to a statute listing certain rights of parents and guardians of public-school children and re-enact the law as it was originally enacted by Initiative to the Legislature 2081. Should this measure be enacted into law? Yes [ ] No [ ]
plain: Initiative IL26-001 would restore RCW 28A.605.005 to the version originally enacted by Initiative to the Legislature 2081 in 2024.
It would repeal the changes the Legislature made to that statute in the 2025 session.

The restored law lists rights of parents and guardians of public-school children, including reviewing materials and student records, receiving certain notifications, and opting their child out of certain activities.
WA.yes: A yes vote enacts the measure, re-enacting RCW 28A.605.005 as originally passed under Initiative 2081 and repealing the 2025 legislative amendments, effective December 3, 2026.
WA.no: A no vote rejects the measure, so RCW 28A.605.005 stays in its current form, including the amendments the Legislature made in 2025.
WA.fiscal: Office of Financial Management fiscal impact statement: the initiative "would have no fiscal impact on the state. Local school districts may incur minor costs to update policies and procedures, but this fiscal impact is indeterminate." The initiative would not impact state or local revenue.

WA.title: Initiative Measure No. IL26-638 - An Act Relating to Defending Equity in Interscholastic Sports (Initiative to the Legislature)
WA.ballot_label: Initiative Measure No. IL26-638 concerns participation in athletics at K-12 schools. This measure would prohibit students it defines as "biologically male" from competing in certain school athletic activities intended for female students only. It would require verification of biological sex by students' healthcare providers. Should this measure be enacted into law? Yes [ ] No [ ]
plain: Initiative IL26-638 would require policies barring students it defines as "biologically male" from competing with or against female students in certain interschool athletic activities intended for female students only.
Students who take part in those activities would have to provide a statement from their health care provider verifying the student's biological sex.
Verification would be based on reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels, and the rules would apply to both individual and team competitions.
WA.yes: A yes vote enacts the measure, requiring the athletic eligibility restrictions and health care provider sex verification described in the ballot title, effective December 3, 2026.
WA.no: A no vote rejects the measure, so no new statewide restriction or verification requirement for female-only interschool athletics is added to state law.
WA.fiscal: Office of Financial Management fiscal impact statement: the Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction would incur a one-time cost of approximately $21,000 in state fiscal year 2026 to update existing guidelines. Local school districts would likely also incur costs to revise existing policies, procedures, rules, and other requirements, but that fiscal impact is indeterminate. The initiative would not impact state or local revenue.

IN.title: Public Question #1 - constitutional amendment concerning bail (Senate Joint Resolution 1, 2026; first passage as SJR 1, 2023)
IN.ballot_label: Currently, under the Constitution of the State of Indiana, a person charged with murder or treason is not entitled to be released on bail if the proof is evident or the presumption strong. Shall the Constitution of the State of Indiana be amended to provide that a person charged with an offense other than murder or treason is not entitled to bail if: (1) the proof is evident or the presumption strong; and (2) the state proves by clear and convincing evidence that no release conditions will reasonably protect the safety of any other person or the community. (This question concerns Article 1, Section 17 of the Constitution of the State of Indiana.)
plain: Today the Indiana Constitution says every offense except murder and treason can be released on bail.

This amendment would let a court deny bail for other charges when the evidence of guilt is strong and the state shows by clear and convincing evidence that no release conditions would reasonably protect another person or the community.
It changes Article 1, Section 17 of the Indiana Constitution and takes effect only if a majority of the voters who vote on it approve it.
IN.yes: A yes vote amends the Indiana Constitution so that a court may deny bail for offenses other than murder or treason when both listed conditions are met.
IN.no: A no vote leaves Article 1, Section 17 unchanged, so all offenses except murder and treason remain bailable under the state constitution.
IN.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate is printed with public questions on the Indiana ballot, and no official statewide fiscal estimate for this amendment was found published as of Sept 22, 2026.

IN.title: Public Question #2 - constitutional amendment on town and city court judges (House Joint Resolution 1, 2025; first passage as HJR 6, 2023)
IN.ballot_label: Shall the Constitution of the State of Indiana be amended to permit the judge of a city or town court to reside in: (1) the county in which the court is located; or (2) the bordering county closest to the city or town in which the court is located? (This question concerns Article 6, Section 6 of the Constitution of the State of Indiana.)
plain: Under current law a city or town court judge in Indiana must live in the city or town that the court serves.
This amendment would let that judge live anywhere in the county where the court sits, or in the bordering county closest to that city or town.
It changes Article 6, Section 6 of the Indiana Constitution and takes effect only if a majority of the voters who vote on it approve it.
IN.yes: A yes vote amends the Indiana Constitution to let a city or town court judge live in the court's county or in the closest bordering county.
IN.no: A no vote keeps the current constitutional rule that a city or town court judge must live in the city or town where the court is located.
IN.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate is printed with public questions on the Indiana ballot, and no official statewide fiscal estimate for this amendment was found published as of Sept 22, 2026.

IA.title: Iowa Constitutional Amendment - Taxation Limitations (House Joint Resolution 2006, 90th G.A. / Senate Joint Resolution 11, 91st G.A.)
IA.ballot_label: Public Measure 1 - Iowa Constitutional Amendment - Taxation Limitations. Summary as printed on the county ballot: 'Provides that any bill that increases the individual income tax rate or the corporate income tax rate, or the rate of any other type of tax based upon income or legal and special reserves, shall require the affirmative votes of at least two-thirds of the members elected to each house of the general assembly for passage.' The ballot also prints the amendment itself, adding ARTICLE XIII. TAXATION LIMITATIONS, Section 1, 'Two-thirds majority vote for state tax law changes,' which applies the same two-thirds requirement to a bill establishing a new state tax on any type of income or legal and special reserves, exempts taxes imposed by local governments, requires any challenge to proper enactment to be filed within one year, and requires each affected bill to contain a separate provision describing these enactment requirements.
plain: Today the Iowa Legislature can raise state income tax rates with a simple majority vote in each chamber.

It would amend the constitution to require at least two-thirds of the members elected to each chamber to raise the individual or corporate income tax rate, raise any other tax based on income or on legal and special reserves, or create a new state tax on that income.

The two-thirds requirement would not apply to taxes imposed by cities, counties, or other local governments, and any lawsuit claiming a bill was not properly enacted would have to be filed within one year.
IA.yes: A yes vote adds Article XIII to the Iowa Constitution, requiring a two-thirds vote of each legislative chamber to raise state income tax rates or create a new income-based state tax.
IA.no: A no vote makes no change, so the Legislature can continue to change state income tax rates by a simple majority vote in each chamber.
IA.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate is printed on the Iowa ballot for a constitutional amendment, and no official state fiscal estimate for this measure was published as of Sept 22, 2026.

KS.title: A PROPOSITION to amend section 1 of article 5 of the constitution of the state of Kansas to require individuals to be citizens of the United States, at least 18 years of age and a resident of the voting area in which such person seeks to vote in order to vote in this state.
KS.ballot_label: Explanatory statement. This amendment would clarify only a person who is a citizen of the United States is eligible to vote in this state. A vote for this proposition would clarify that only a person who is a citizen of the United States is eligible to vote in this state. A vote against this proposition would make no change to the Constitution of the State of Kansas, and the language concerning voter qualifications would remain the same. (Printed with the text of the amendment, which rewrites Section 1 of Article 5 to read: 'No person shall be deemed a qualified elector unless such person: (1) Is a citizen of the United States; (2) has attained the age of eighteen years; and (3) except as provided in subsection (b) or (c), resides in the voting area in which such person seeks to vote.' Subsections (b) and (c), which allow certain former residents to vote for president and vice president or in a former voting area, are retained.)
plain: Section 1 of Article 5 of the Kansas Constitution now says that every U.S. citizen who is at least eighteen and who lives in the voting area is a qualified elector.

This amendment rewrites that section to state that no person is a qualified elector unless the person is a U.S. citizen, is at least eighteen years old, and lives in the voting area where the person seeks to vote.
It keeps the existing exceptions that let certain people who have moved still vote for president and vice president, or vote in their former voting area.
KS.yes: A yes vote changes Section 1 of Article 5 of the Kansas Constitution so it states that a person is not a qualified elector unless the person is a U.S. citizen, is at least eighteen, and resides in the voting area.
KS.no: A no vote makes no change to the Kansas Constitution, and the current voter-qualification language stays the same.
KS.fiscal: The Legislative Research Department's supplemental note on HCR 5004 states under Fiscal Information: 'No fiscal note was available at the time the House Committee took action on the resolution. [Note: The representative of the Secretary of State indicated that there is an estimated cost of $50,000, all from the State General Fund, to publish public notice of Constitutional Resolutions.]' No fiscal estimate is printed on the ballot itself.

MI.title: A proposal to convene a constitutional convention for the purpose of drafting a general revision of the state constitution
MI.ballot_label: A proposal to convene a constitutional convention for the purpose of drafting a general revision of the state constitution. Shall a convention of elected delegates be convened in 2027 to draft a general revision of the state constitution for presentation to the state's voters for their approval or rejection?
plain: The Michigan Constitution requires this question to be placed before voters automatically every sixteen years; it was last asked in 2010.
If it passes, voters would elect delegates who would meet in a convention in 2027 to write a general revision of the state constitution.
Anything the convention produces would come back to Michigan voters at a later election for a separate yes-or-no vote before it could take effect.
MI.yes: A yes vote calls a convention of elected delegates to meet in 2027 to draft a general revision of the Michigan Constitution, which voters would later approve or reject.
MI.no: A no vote means no constitutional convention is held and the current Michigan Constitution remains in effect unchanged.
MI.fiscal: Michigan does not print an official fiscal estimate with statewide ballot proposals, and no official state fiscal estimate for this proposal was published as of Sept 22, 2026.

MI.title: A proposed initiated law to prohibit campaign contributions from certain regulated utilities and government contractors and apply campaign finance laws and regulations to additional types of political communications
MI.ballot_label: A PROPOSED INITIATED LAW TO PROHIBIT CAMPAIGN CONTRIBUTIONS FROM CERTAIN REGULATED UTILITIES AND GOVERNMENT CONTRACTORS AND APPLY CAMPAIGN FINANCE LAWS AND REGULATIONS TO ADDITIONAL TYPES OF POLITICAL COMMUNICATIONS. This proposed law would: Prohibit regulated electric and gas utilities, contractors with over $250,000 annually in government contracts, and people and organizations with substantial connections to these utilities/contractors from making direct or indirect campaign contributions to those who run for or hold offices that impact them. Expand laws regulating spending on political communications, including those requiring disclosing donor information, to apply to communications clearly identifying candidates or ballot questions, even if they do not expressly advocate voting for/against them. Expressly apply the law requiring disclosure of who paid for political communications to internet political communications. Should this proposal be adopted?
plain: This initiated law would bar regulated electric and gas utilities, and businesses holding more than $250,000 a year in government contracts, from giving campaign contributions to candidates and officeholders whose offices affect them.
The ban would also reach people and organizations with substantial connections to those utilities and contractors, and would cover indirect contributions as well as direct ones.

It would extend Michigan's campaign finance and donor-disclosure rules to political messages that clearly identify a candidate or ballot question even without expressly urging a vote, and would apply the 'paid for by' disclosure rule to internet political communications.
MI.yes: A yes vote enacts the initiated law, adding the contribution prohibitions and the expanded disclosure requirements to Michigan campaign finance law.
MI.no: A no vote rejects the initiated law and leaves Michigan's current campaign finance and disclosure rules unchanged.
MI.fiscal: Michigan does not print an official fiscal estimate with statewide ballot proposals, and no official state fiscal estimate for this proposal was published as of Sept 22, 2026.

MN.number: Constitutional Amendment - Increasing Funding to School Districts
MN.title: Increasing Funding to School Districts
MN.ballot_label: Shall the Minnesota Constitution be amended to increase the funding going to all school districts from the permanent school fund, which is a fund that supports school districts without raising individual income or property taxes, effective July 1, 2027? (Ballot instruction printed with the question: 'Failure to vote on a constitutional amendment will have the same effect as voting no on the amendment.')
plain: The permanent school fund is a state investment fund whose earnings are paid out to every Minnesota school district each year.
This amendment changes Article XI, Section 8 of the Minnesota Constitution so the fund must be managed to provide annual distributions while preserving the fund's purchasing power over time.
If approved, the change takes effect July 1, 2027 and would send more money to school districts each year without raising individual income or property taxes.
MN.yes: A yes vote amends Article XI, Section 8 of the Minnesota Constitution to change how the permanent school fund is managed so that larger annual distributions go to school districts beginning July 1, 2027.
MN.no: A no vote leaves the current constitutional language governing the permanent school fund unchanged; leaving the question blank has the same effect as a no vote.
MN.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate is printed on the Minnesota ballot for a constitutional amendment, and no official statewide fiscal estimate was published as of Sept 22, 2026; the Attorney General's statement of purpose and effect, published with the Secretary of State's amendment page, is the official explanatory document.

MO.title: Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to: Repeal the 2024 voter-approved Amendment providing reproductive healthcare rights, including abortion through fetal viability; Allow abortions for rape and incest (under twelve-weeks' gestation), emergencies, and fetal anomalies; Allow legislation regulating abortion; Ensure parental consent for minors' abortions; Prohibit gender transition procedures for minors?
MO.ballot_label: Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to: Repeal the 2024 voter-approved Amendment providing reproductive healthcare rights, including abortion through fetal viability; Allow abortions for rape and incest (under twelve-weeks' gestation), emergencies, and fetal anomalies; Allow legislation regulating abortion; Ensure parental consent for minors' abortions; Prohibit gender transition procedures for minors?
plain: This amendment would repeal Article I, Section 36, the reproductive healthcare rights amendment Missouri voters approved in November 2024.

In its place it would allow abortion only in a medical emergency, for a fetal anomaly, or in cases of rape or incest before twelve weeks of pregnancy, would let the legislature pass laws regulating abortion, and would require parental consent for a minor's abortion.
It would also prohibit gender transition procedures for people under eighteen.
MO.yes: A yes vote repeals the 2024 reproductive healthcare rights amendment and writes the listed abortion limits, the parental-consent requirement, and the ban on gender transition procedures for minors into the Missouri Constitution.
MO.no: A no vote leaves the 2024 reproductive healthcare rights amendment in the Missouri Constitution and makes no change to it.
MO.fiscal: Official Fiscal Note Summary printed on the ballot: 'State governmental entities estimate no costs or savings. Greene County estimates it may experience an unknown increase in tax revenue. Other local governmental entities estimate no costs or savings.'

MO.title: Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to: expand the initiative and referendum petition process by making it a fundamental right; allow courts to revise ballot summaries through lawsuits; prohibit the legislature from weakening initiative or referendum powers; prohibit the legislature from changing or repealing laws enacted through the initiative process, or passing laws similar to those rejected by referendum, without approval from at least 80% of both chambers; and preserve existing majority vote and signature requirements for initiative and referendum petitions?
MO.ballot_label: Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to: expand the initiative and referendum petition process by making it a fundamental right; allow courts to revise ballot summaries through lawsuits; prohibit the legislature from weakening initiative or referendum powers; prohibit the legislature from changing or repealing laws enacted through the initiative process, or passing laws similar to those rejected by referendum, without approval from at least 80% of both chambers; and preserve existing majority vote and signature requirements for initiative and referendum petitions?
plain: This amendment would make the people's power to propose initiatives and referendums a fundamental right in the Missouri Constitution.
It would bar the legislature from passing laws that weaken those petition powers, and would let a court revise a ballot summary in a lawsuit.

It would take a vote of at least 80% of both legislative chambers to change or repeal a law voters passed, or to pass a law similar to one voters rejected. The existing majority-vote and signature rules for petitions stay the same.
MO.yes: A yes vote adds these initiative and referendum protections to the Missouri Constitution, including the 80% legislative vote requirement to alter voter-approved initiative laws.
MO.no: A no vote leaves the current constitutional provisions on initiative and referendum petitions unchanged.
MO.fiscal: Official Fiscal Note Summary printed on the ballot: 'State and local governmental entities estimate no costs or savings.'

MO.title: Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to establish a permanent public endowment fund to support state government instead of taxing Missouri residents, prohibit the General Assembly from appropriating or diverting the fund, and eliminate state-imposed taxes once the fund generates sufficient revenue to replace them?
MO.ballot_label: Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to establish a permanent public endowment fund to support state government instead of taxing Missouri residents, prohibit the General Assembly from appropriating or diverting the fund, and eliminate state-imposed taxes once the fund generates sufficient revenue to replace them?
plain: This amendment would create a permanent public endowment fund in the Missouri Constitution, referred to in the Secretary of State's Fair Ballot Language as the 'Show-Me Prosperity Fund,' to support state government.
The General Assembly would be barred from appropriating money out of the fund or diverting it to other uses.
State-imposed taxes would be eliminated once the fund generates enough revenue to replace what those taxes bring in.
MO.yes: A yes vote creates the permanent endowment fund in the Missouri Constitution, shields it from legislative appropriation or diversion, and requires state-imposed taxes to end once the fund can replace that revenue.
MO.no: A no vote makes no change, and Missouri continues to fund state government through its existing tax system.
MO.fiscal: Official Fiscal Note Summary printed on the ballot: 'State and local governmental entities estimate no costs or savings.'

MO.title: Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to support law enforcement by preserving the right of citizens to elect a county sheriff, prohibiting the removal of a county sheriff except by a writ of quo warranto, and recognizing the office of sheriff as part of the administration of justice?
MO.ballot_label: Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to support law enforcement by preserving the right of citizens to elect a county sheriff, prohibiting the removal of a county sheriff except by a writ of quo warranto, and recognizing the office of sheriff as part of the administration of justice?
plain: This amendment would put into the Missouri Constitution the right of voters in each county to elect their county sheriff.
It would allow a county sheriff to be removed from office only through a court proceeding called a writ of quo warranto.
It would also recognize the office of sheriff in the constitution as part of the administration of justice.
MO.yes: A yes vote writes the elected office of county sheriff into the Missouri Constitution and limits removal of a sheriff to a quo warranto court proceeding.
MO.no: A no vote leaves the office of county sheriff governed by existing Missouri statutes rather than the constitution.
MO.fiscal: Official Fiscal Note Summary printed on the ballot: 'State and local governmental entities estimate no costs or savings.'

MO.title: Do the people of the state of Missouri approve the act of the General Assembly entitled 'House Bill No. 1 (2025 Second Extraordinary Session),' which repeals Missouri's existing congressional plan, and replaces it with new congressional boundaries that keep more counties intact?
MO.ballot_label: Do the people of the state of Missouri approve the act of the General Assembly entitled 'House Bill No. 1 (2025 Second Extraordinary Session),' which repeals Missouri's existing congressional plan, and replaces it with new congressional boundaries that keep more counties intact?
plain: This is a veto referendum: voters decide whether a law the General Assembly already passed, House Bill 1 from the 2025 Second Extraordinary Session, takes effect.
House Bill 1 repeals Missouri's existing congressional district plan and replaces it with new congressional district boundaries.
Only congressional district lines are at issue; no other state law is changed by this question.
MO.yes: A yes vote approves House Bill 1 (2025 Second Extraordinary Session), allowing the congressional district boundaries it draws to take effect.
MO.no: A no vote rejects House Bill 1, so Missouri's previously enacted congressional district plan remains in place.
MO.fiscal: Official Fiscal Note Summary printed on the ballot: 'State and local governmental entities estimate no costs or savings.'

NE.title: Initiative Measure 440, Proposed by Initiative Petition. Object statement: "The object of this petition is to amend the Nebraska Constitution to state that laws may be enacted allowing sports wagers to be placed within the State of Nebraska through an Internet-based platform offered by an authorized gaming operator."
NE.ballot_label: A vote "FOR" will amend the Nebraska Constitution to authorize the enactment of laws to allow persons located within Nebraska to place sports wagers through an Internet-based platform when offered by an authorized gaming operator conducting games of chance within a licensed racetrack enclosure in Nebraska. A vote "AGAINST" means the Nebraska Constitution will not be amended in this manner. Shall the Nebraska Constitution be amended to authorize the enactment of laws allowing persons located within Nebraska to place sports wagers through an Internet-based platform when offered by an authorized gaming operator conducting games of chance within a licensed racetrack enclosure in Nebraska? For / Against
plain: This measure would change the Nebraska Constitution so that state laws may allow sports bets to be placed over the internet.
Only a gaming operator already authorized to run games of chance inside a licensed racetrack enclosure in Nebraska could offer those internet bets.
A person would have to be located within Nebraska at the time the wager is placed.
NE.yes: A vote FOR amends the Nebraska Constitution to authorize the Legislature to enact laws allowing people located in Nebraska to place sports wagers through an internet-based platform offered by an authorized racetrack gaming operator.
NE.no: A vote AGAINST leaves the Nebraska Constitution unchanged, so the constitution would continue to not authorize laws permitting internet-based sports wagering.
NE.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept. 22, 2026. Nebraska law does not require a fiscal note for ballot measures, and the Secretary of State's 2026 informational pamphlet contains only the ballot title and text, the full measure text, and proponent/opponent arguments.

NE.title: Initiative Measure 441, Proposed by Initiative Petition. Object statement: "The object of this petition is to enact a statute allowing sports wagers to be placed within the State of Nebraska through Internet-based platforms offered by an authorized gaming operator, or its contracted platform provider, and regulate such sports wagers."
NE.ballot_label: A vote "FOR" will enact statutes allowing persons located within Nebraska to place sports wagers through an Internet-based platform when offered by an authorized gaming operator conducting games of chance within a licensed racetrack enclosure in Nebraska or the operator's platform provider, and regulating such sports wagers. A vote "AGAINST" means no such statutes will be enacted. Shall statutes be enacted that: (1) Allow persons located within Nebraska to place sports wagers through an Internet-based platform when offered by an authorized gaming operator conducting games of chance within a licensed racetrack enclosure in Nebraska or the operator's platform provider; and (2) Regulate such sports wagers? For / Against
plain: This measure would write into state law the rules that let people located in Nebraska place sports bets through an internet platform.
The platform would have to be offered by an authorized racetrack gaming operator or by that operator's contracted platform provider.
The new statutes would also set up how online sports wagering is regulated in the state.
NE.yes: A vote FOR enacts statutes permitting internet-based sports wagering by people located in Nebraska through authorized racetrack gaming operators or their platform providers, and establishing the rules regulating that wagering.
NE.no: A vote AGAINST means those statutes are not enacted and Nebraska statutes would continue to not authorize or regulate internet-based sports wagering.
NE.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept. 22, 2026. Nebraska law does not require a fiscal note for ballot measures, and the Secretary of State's 2026 informational pamphlet contains only the ballot title and text, the full measure text, and proponent/opponent arguments.

NE.title: Initiative Measure 442, Proposed by Initiative Petition. Object statement: "The object of this petition is to amend the Nebraska Constitution to establish constitutional protections for sex-separate athletics to ensure equal access to athletic opportunities for females."
NE.ballot_label: A vote "FOR" will amend the Nebraska Constitution to provide: (1) Schools must expressly designate each athletic team or sport as one of the following based on biological sex: (a) Males, men, or boys; (b) females, women, or girls; or (c) coed or mixed; and (2) Athletic teams or sports designated for females, women, or girls shall not be open to students of the male sex. The amendment would apply to all athletic teams or sports sponsored by public schools or postsecondary educational institutions, and private schools or educational institutions whose athletic teams or sports compete against public schools or institutions. A vote "AGAINST" means the Nebraska Constitution will not be amended in this manner. Shall the Nebraska Constitution be amended to provide: (1) Schools must expressly designate each athletic team or sport as one of the following based on biological sex: (a) Males, men, or boys; (b) females, women, or girls; or (c) coed or mixed; and (2) Athletic teams or sports designated for females, women, or girls shall not be open to students of the male sex? The amendment would apply to all athletic teams or sports sponsored by public schools or postsecondary educational institutions, and private schools or educational institutions whose athletic teams or sports compete against public schools or institutions. For / Against
plain: This measure would put in the Nebraska Constitution a requirement that schools label every athletic team or sport, based on biological sex, as male, female, or coed/mixed.
Teams or sports labeled for females, women, or girls could not be open to students of the male sex.
The requirement would cover public schools and postsecondary institutions, plus private schools whose teams compete against public ones.
NE.yes: A vote FOR amends the Nebraska Constitution to require sex-based designation of school athletic teams and to bar students of the male sex from teams designated for females, women, or girls at covered schools.
NE.no: A vote AGAINST leaves the Nebraska Constitution unchanged, so no constitutional designation or eligibility requirement for school athletic teams would be added.
NE.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept. 22, 2026. Nebraska law does not require a fiscal note for ballot measures, and the Secretary of State's 2026 informational pamphlet contains only the ballot title and text, the full measure text, and proponent/opponent arguments.

NE.number: LR19CA (constitutional amendment referred by the Legislature; ballot number not published by the Secretary of State as of Sept. 22, 2026)
NE.title: Legislative Resolution 19CA (2025) - proposed constitutional amendment on legislative term limits, ballot statement approved by the Executive Board of the Legislative Council on June 10, 2026
NE.ballot_label: Ballot Statement - LR19CA (2025): A vote FOR will amend the state constitution to increase the term limit for state legislators from two consecutive four-year terms (eight years) to three consecutive four-year terms (12 years). A vote AGAINST will not amend the Nebraska Constitution, so the current limit of two consecutive four-year terms will remain in effect. State legislators will continue to be ineligible for office in the Legislature for four years after serving two consecutive terms.
plain: This amendment would change how long a person can serve in the Nebraska Legislature without a break.
The limit would go from two consecutive four-year terms, or eight years, to three consecutive four-year terms, or 12 years.
Under current law a senator must sit out four years after two consecutive terms, and that waiting period would apply after three terms instead.
NE.yes: A vote FOR amends the Nebraska Constitution to raise the consecutive-term limit for state legislators from two four-year terms to three four-year terms.
NE.no: A vote AGAINST leaves the current limit of two consecutive four-year terms in place, with legislators ineligible for the Legislature for four years after serving two consecutive terms.
NE.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept. 22, 2026; the Secretary of State posted only the Executive Board's approved ballot statement language for LR19CA.

ND.title: Constitutional Measure No. 1 (House Concurrent Resolution No. 3003, 2025 Session Laws, Ch. 614)
ND.ballot_label: This constitutional measure would amend and reenact section 9 of article III and section 16 of article IV of the Constitution of North Dakota. The proposed amendment would require constitutional amendments submitted to the electors, by resolution adopted by the legislative assembly proposing a constitutional amendment and each initiative petition and measure proposing a constitutional amendment, to receive an affirmative vote of at least sixty percent of those voting on the question for enactment. The estimated fiscal impact of this measure is none. Yes - Means you approve the measure as summarized above. No - Means you reject the measure as summarized above.
plain: This measure would change how many votes it takes to approve a change to the North Dakota Constitution.
Amendments placed on the ballot by the Legislative Assembly and amendments proposed by initiative petition would each need at least 60 percent of the votes cast on the question.
Constitutional amendments now pass with a simple majority, so this would set a higher bar for future amendments.
ND.yes: A yes vote approves the amendment, requiring every future constitutional amendment, whether legislature-referred or initiated, to receive at least 60 percent of the votes cast on the question to be enacted.
ND.no: A no vote rejects the amendment, so constitutional amendments would continue to be enacted by a simple majority of those voting on the question.
ND.fiscal: Official ballot language and the Secretary of State's analysis both state: "The estimated fiscal impact of this measure is none."

ND.title: Initiated Constitutional Measure No. 2 (initiated constitutional measure relating to school meals, placed on the ballot by petitions circulated by a sponsoring committee)
ND.ballot_label: This initiated measure amendment would amend and add a new section to article VIII of the North Dakota Constitution. It would mandate all public school districts, public schools, and public charter schools to provide one breakfast and one lunch each school day to enrolled students at no cost to the student, parent, or guardians. It would allow nonpublic schools, Bureau of Indian Education schools, and other tribal schools the option to provide the same. It would require the State of North Dakota to reimburse school districts and schools at one hundred percent of the current rates used by the state for free meals, and the rate shall be adjusted annually for inflation. It would require the legislative assembly to identify a source of funds for reimbursement and if a source of funds is unable to be identified, reimbursement funds would be appropriated from the legacy earnings fund. This amendment would supersede any other part of the constitution that conflicts with it. The estimated fiscal impact of this measure is a $124.3 million to $134.3 million increase in ongoing biennial expenditures for the 2027-2029 biennium and will be adjusted for inflation every year after that. Yes - Means you approve the measure as summarized above. No - Means you reject the measure as summarized above.
plain: This measure would require every public school district, public school, and public charter school to serve one breakfast and one lunch each school day at no cost to students or their families.
Nonpublic schools, Bureau of Indian Education schools, and other tribal schools could choose to offer the same free meals.

The state would reimburse schools at 100 percent of the current state rates for free meals, adjusted yearly for inflation, with money from the legacy earnings fund if the Legislative Assembly does not identify another source.
ND.yes: A yes vote approves the amendment, adding a section to Article VIII of the North Dakota Constitution that requires free school breakfast and lunch at public schools and obligates the state to reimburse schools for the cost.
ND.no: A no vote rejects the amendment, so the constitution would not require free school meals or state reimbursement for them.
ND.fiscal: Official ballot language: "The estimated fiscal impact of this measure is a $124.3 million to $134.3 million increase in ongoing biennial expenditures for the 2027-2029 biennium and will be adjusted for inflation every year after that." The Legislative Council's July 2026 report (N.D.C.C. 16.1-01-17) gives the Department of Public Instruction's 2027-29 estimate as $124 million to $134 million for the cost of free meals plus $300,000 in departmental administrative costs.

SD.title: An Amendment to the South Dakota Constitution that Repeals Expanded Medicaid Coverage if Federal Funding for the Program Drops below 90%. (HJR 5001, 2025)
SD.ballot_label: Title: An Amendment to the South Dakota Constitution that Repeals Expanded Medicaid Coverage if Federal Funding for the Program Drops below 90%. Attorney General Explanation: Medicaid is a program, funded by the State and the federal government, to provide medical coverage for low-income children, pregnant women, disabled individuals, and the elderly. In the 2022 General Election the voters approved Constitutional Amendment D, which expanded Medicaid eligibility in South Dakota. Amendment D requires the State to also provide Medicaid benefits to anyone over the age of 18 and under 65 whose income is at or below 133% of the federal property level, plus 5% of the federal poverty level for the applicable family size. Currently, federal law requires the federal government to fund 90% of South Dakota's Medicaid expansion. This proposed Constitutional Amendment ends the expanded Medicaid coverage if the federal funding for expansion drops below 90%. If federal funding drops below that 90% threshold, Medicaid coverage will once again only apply to low-income children, pregnant women, disabled individuals, and the elderly. Vote "Yes" to adopt the amendment. Vote "No" to leave the Constitution as it is. The text of this constitutional amendment is two pages long with two sections.
plain: South Dakota voters added Medicaid expansion to the state constitution in 2022, covering adults ages 18 to 64 with incomes at or below 133 percent of the federal poverty level plus 5 percent.
This amendment would end that expanded coverage if the federal government's share of the expansion cost falls below 90 percent.
If that happened, Medicaid would again cover only low-income children, pregnant women, disabled individuals, and the elderly.
SD.yes: A yes vote adopts the amendment, so expanded Medicaid coverage would end automatically if federal funding for the expansion drops below 90 percent.
SD.no: A no vote leaves the constitution as it is, so the state would remain constitutionally required to provide expanded Medicaid coverage regardless of the federal funding share.
SD.fiscal: No official fiscal note was published for this amendment as of Sept. 22, 2026; the Secretary of State's 2026 ballot questions page lists only the Attorney General's draft and final statements, and the official 2026 Ballot Question Pamphlet contains no fiscal note for it.

SD.title: An Amendment to the South Dakota Constitution Clarifying that an Individual Must Be a Citizen of the United States to be Eligible to Vote. (SJR 503, 2025)
SD.ballot_label: Title: An Amendment to the South Dakota Constitution Clarifying that an Individual Must Be a Citizen of the United States to be Eligible to Vote. Attorney General Explanation: Article VII, Section 2 of the South Dakota Constitution defines who is qualified to vote in state elections. Among these qualifications are age, residency, and United States citizenship requirements. Article VII, Section 2 also establishes that individuals may be disqualified from voting because of mental incompetence or a felony conviction. This constitutional amendment adds people who are not United States citizens to the list of individuals disqualified from voting, clarifying the existing requirement that only citizens may vote in state elections. Vote "Yes" to adopt the amendment. Vote "No" to leave the Constitution as it is. The text of this constitutional amendment is one page long with two sections.
plain: The South Dakota Constitution already lists United States citizenship among the qualifications for voting in state elections.
This amendment would add people who are not United States citizens to the constitution's list of individuals disqualified from voting.
The Attorney General describes the change as clarifying the citizenship requirement that already exists.
SD.yes: A yes vote adopts the amendment, adding non-citizens to the constitutional list of people disqualified from voting in state elections.
SD.no: A no vote leaves the constitution as it is, with citizenship listed as a voter qualification but non-citizens not named in the list of disqualifications.
SD.fiscal: No official fiscal note was published for this amendment as of Sept. 22, 2026; the Secretary of State's 2026 ballot questions page lists only the Attorney General's draft and final statements, and the official 2026 Ballot Question Pamphlet contains no fiscal note for it.

SD.title: An Amendment to the South Dakota Constitution Establishing the Trust for Unclaimed Property Fund. (SJR 505, 2025)
SD.ballot_label: Title: An Amendment to the South Dakota Constitution Establishing the Trust for Unclaimed Property Fund. Attorney General Explanation: Under South Dakota statute, intangible property is presumed to be abandoned if it remains unclaimed by the owner for more than three years after it became payable or distributable. Examples of intangible property are traveler's checks, money orders, bank deposits, refunds, stocks, funds owed under a life insurance policy, and property held in a safe deposit box. Abandoned intangible property is transferred to the State Treasurer to hold while waiting for the owner to claim it. The State Treasurer must provide public notice of the abandoned property. This proposed constitutional amendment establishes a trust fund where unclaimed abandoned property will be deposited. Portions of the interest and income from this fund will be distributed into the general fund for the benefit of the state. This proposed amendment requires the Legislature to determine the amount to be distributed that promotes the growth of the trust fund and the distributed amount. Vote "Yes" to adopt the amendment. Vote "No" to leave the Constitution as it is. The text of this constitutional amendment is two pages long containing two sections.
plain: Intangible property that goes unclaimed for more than three years is treated as abandoned and turned over to the State Treasurer to hold for the owner.
This amendment would create a constitutional trust fund where that unclaimed abandoned property is deposited.
Portions of the interest and income from the fund would be distributed to the state general fund, with the Legislature setting the amount in a way that also grows the fund.
SD.yes: A yes vote adopts the amendment, creating a constitutional trust for unclaimed property and directing part of its interest and income to the state general fund in amounts set by the Legislature.
SD.no: A no vote leaves the constitution as it is, so unclaimed abandoned property would continue to be handled under existing statutes without a constitutional trust fund.
SD.fiscal: No official fiscal note was published for this amendment as of Sept. 22, 2026; the Secretary of State's 2026 ballot questions page lists only the Attorney General's draft and final statements, and the official 2026 Ballot Question Pamphlet contains no fiscal note for it.

SD.title: An Amendment to the South Dakota Constitution Requiring that a Proposed Constitutional Amendment or Revision Receive an Affirmative Vote of Sixty Percent of the Votes Cast. (HJR 5003, 2025)
SD.ballot_label: Title: An Amendment to the South Dakota Constitution Requiring that a Proposed Constitutional Amendment or Revision Receive an Affirmative Vote of Sixty Percent of the Votes Cast. Attorney General Explanation: The State Constitution provides that any proposed constitutional amendment or revision must be submitted to the voters for approval. Currently, a proposed constitutional amendment or revision becomes part of the Constitution if approved by a majority of the votes cast. This proposed Constitutional Amendment increases the number of votes required for a proposed constitutional amendment or revision to become part of the Constitution. If passed, further constitutional amendments must receive an affirmative vote of sixty percent of the votes cast to be implemented. Vote "Yes" to adopt the amendment. Vote "No" to leave the Constitution as it is. The text of this constitutional amendment is one page long containing two sections.
plain: A proposed change to the South Dakota Constitution now becomes part of the constitution if a majority of the votes cast approve it.
This amendment would raise that requirement to 60 percent of the votes cast.
The higher threshold would apply to future proposed constitutional amendments and revisions.
SD.yes: A yes vote adopts the amendment, requiring future constitutional amendments or revisions to receive an affirmative vote of 60 percent of the votes cast to take effect.
SD.no: A no vote leaves the constitution as it is, so constitutional amendments and revisions would continue to take effect with a majority of the votes cast.
SD.fiscal: No official fiscal note was published for this amendment as of Sept. 22, 2026; the Secretary of State's 2026 ballot questions page lists only the Attorney General's draft and final statements, and the official 2026 Ballot Question Pamphlet contains no fiscal note for it.

OH.title: Require photo identification to vote
OH.ballot_label:
Heads up: we could not confirm the exact certified ballot wording. Ohio's Secretary of State website could not be read automatically on September 22, 2026, so the wording below comes from several reports of the Ballot Board's August 3, 2026 certification and from the resolution the legislature passed. Read the official text at https://www.ohiosos.gov/assets/certified-ballot-language-08-03-2026.pdf before you rely on it.

The certified title says the amendment would require voters "to present photo identification in order to vote." The certified language requires voters "to present an approved form of government-issued photo identification in order to vote"; lets state law provide another way to verify the identity of a voter who has a sincere religious objection to being photographed and so does not have an approved photo ID; and requires voters who do not vote in person to provide an approved government-issued photo ID, unless the law lets them give a signature plus at least one other specified unique identifier.

The text that would be added to the Ohio Constitution reads: 'Section 5. (A) Electors shall provide photo identification in order to vote in person at a polling place or other voting location designated by law, in accordance with laws passed by the general assembly, except that the laws may provide an alternative method of verifying the identity of an elector who does not have photo identification because the elector has a sincere religious objection to being photographed. (B) At a minimum, and in accordance with laws passed by the general assembly, electors shall provide photo identification or, if authorized by law, a signature and at least one other unique identifier in order to vote by any other method authorized by law.' The resolution adds that if a majority of electors voting on the proposal adopt it, the new Section 5 takes effect immediately.
plain: This amendment would place Ohio's photo ID requirement for voting into the state constitution instead of leaving it only in state law.

People voting in person would have to show an unexpired government-issued photo ID from a specific list, such as an Ohio driver's license or state ID card, a U.S. passport or passport card, or a U.S. military, Ohio National Guard, or Veterans Affairs ID card.

People voting by another method would have to show photo ID or, if state law allows, give a signature plus at least one other unique identifier, and state law could set up a different way to verify identity for a voter with a sincere religious objection to being photographed.
OH.yes: A yes vote enacts Section 5 of Article V of the Ohio Constitution, making the photo identification requirement for voting a constitutional requirement that takes effect immediately upon adoption.
OH.no: A no vote does not enact Section 5 of Article V, leaving Ohio's photo identification requirement for voting in statute, where the General Assembly can change or repeal it.
OH.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept 22, 2026. No fiscal estimate or cost statement appears among the Secretary of State's certified Issue 3 materials (certified ballot language, certified explanation, arguments for and against), and no Legislative Service Commission fiscal note for Sub. S.J.R. No. 10 was located. No estimate has been produced here.

WI.title: Partial veto - 2025 Senate Joint Resolution 116 (first considered as 2023 Assembly Joint Resolution 112 / 2023 Enrolled Joint Resolution 16): To amend section 10(1)(c) of article V; relating to: prohibiting the governor from using the partial veto to create or increase any tax or fee.
WI.ballot_label: QUESTION 1: "Partial veto. Shall section 10 (1) (c) of article V of the constitution be amended to prohibit the governor, in exercising his or her partial veto authority, from creating or increasing or authorizing the creation or increase of any tax or fee?"
plain: This amendment would change the part of the state constitution that governs the governor's partial veto of spending bills.
It would bar the governor from using that partial veto to create or increase any tax or fee.
It would also bar a partial veto that authorizes local government bodies, such as school districts, to create or increase their own taxes or fees.
WI.yes: A yes vote amends Article V, Section 10(1)(c) of the Wisconsin Constitution so the governor may not use the partial veto to create or increase, or authorize the creation or increase of, any tax or fee.
WI.no: A no vote leaves Article V, Section 10(1)(c) unchanged, keeping the governor's current partial veto authority over appropriation bills.
WI.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept 22, 2026. The statewide Type C Notice of Referendum Election for November 3, 2026 carries an explanatory statement for each question but contains no fiscal estimate, and no separate fiscal estimate was located for the joint resolution. No estimate has been produced here.

WI.title: Freedom to gather in places of worship during an emergency - 2025 Assembly Joint Resolution 10 (first considered as 2023 Senate Joint Resolution 54 / 2023 Enrolled Joint Resolution 11): To amend section 18 of article I of the constitution; relating to: the freedom to gather in places of worship during a state of emergency.
WI.ballot_label: QUESTION 2: "Freedom to gather in places of worship during an emergency. Shall section 18 of article I of the constitution, which deals with religious liberty, be amended to prohibit the state or a political subdivision of the state from ordering the closure of, or forbidding gatherings in, places of worship in response to a state of emergency, including a public health emergency?"
plain: This amendment would add new language to the religious liberty section of the state constitution.
It would stop the state and local governments from ordering places of worship to close during a declared national, state, or local emergency.
It would also stop them from forbidding gatherings at places of worship during such an emergency, including an emergency related to public health.
WI.yes: A yes vote amends Article I, Section 18 of the Wisconsin Constitution to prohibit the state or a political subdivision from ordering the closure of, or forbidding gatherings in, places of worship in response to a state of emergency.
WI.no: A no vote leaves Article I, Section 18 unchanged, so officials may continue to limit gatherings at places of worship during a declared emergency provided religious and secular gatherings are treated the same.
WI.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept 22, 2026. The statewide Type C Notice of Referendum Election for November 3, 2026 carries an explanatory statement for each question but contains no fiscal estimate, and no separate fiscal estimate was located for the joint resolution. No estimate has been produced here.

WI.title: Governmental entity discrimination prohibited - 2025 Assembly Joint Resolution 102 (first considered as 2023 Assembly Joint Resolution 109 / 2023 Enrolled Joint Resolution 15): To create section 27 of article I of the constitution; relating to: prohibiting governmental entity discrimination.
WI.ballot_label: QUESTION 3: "Governmental entity discrimination prohibited. Shall section 27 of article I of the constitution be created to prohibit governmental entities in the state from discriminating against, or granting preferential treatment to, any individual or group on the basis of race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in public employment, public education, public contracting, or public administration?"
plain: This amendment would create a new section of the state constitution covering how government bodies treat people.

It would bar state and local governmental entities - including the University of Wisconsin System, technical colleges, and public school districts - from discriminating against or granting preferential treatment to any individual or group based on race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in public employment, public education, public contracting, or public administration.

It would allow actions needed to keep eligibility for a federal program when losing that eligibility would cost the government body federal funds, and it would allow bona fide sex-based qualifications reasonably necessary to normal operations.
WI.yes: A yes vote creates Article I, Section 27 of the Wisconsin Constitution, prohibiting governmental entities from discriminating against or granting preferential treatment to any individual or group on the basis of race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in public employment, public education, public contracting, or public administration.
WI.no: A no vote does not add Article I, Section 27, leaving existing state and federal equal protection standards as the governing law.
WI.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept 22, 2026. The statewide Type C Notice of Referendum Election for November 3, 2026 carries an explanatory statement for each question but contains no fiscal estimate, and no separate fiscal estimate was located for the joint resolution. No estimate has been produced here.

MA.title: Expanding the Public Records Law
MA.ballot_label: Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? This proposed law would make most records held by the Legislature and the Office of the Governor public records under the Massachusetts Public Records Law. This proposed law would exempt documents related to the development of public policy and communications between legislators and their constituents, if those communications are reasonably related to a constituent's request for assistance in obtaining government-provided benefits or services or interacting with a government agency.
plain: Most records kept by the state Legislature and the Governor's office would become public records under the state Public Records Law.
Documents related to developing public policy would stay exempt from release.
Messages between legislators and constituents about getting government benefits, services, or help dealing with an agency would also stay exempt.
MA.yes: A yes vote would make most records held by the Legislature and the Office of the Governor public records under the Massachusetts Public Records Law.
MA.no: A no vote would make no change to the Massachusetts Public Records Law.
MA.fiscal: Official statement of fiscal consequences (Executive Office of Administration and Finance): 'The proposed law has no discernible material fiscal consequences for state and municipal government finances.'

MA.title: Collective Bargaining for CPCS Employees
MA.ballot_label: Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? This proposed law would specify that employees of the Committee for Public Counsel Services ("CPCS") are permitted to engage in collective bargaining with their employer. It would also require CPCS, after executing a collective bargaining agreement, to request the appropriation necessary to fund such agreement from the Governor.
plain: Employees of the Committee for Public Counsel Services, the state's public defender agency, could form a union and bargain collectively with their employer.
After signing a contract, the agency would have to ask the Governor for the money needed to pay for it.
The law would apply only to CPCS employees and would not change bargaining rules for other workers.
MA.yes: A yes vote would specify that Committee for Public Counsel Services employees may form a union to collectively bargain with their employer.
MA.no: A no vote would make no change to the law governing labor relations for Committee for Public Counsel Service employees.
MA.fiscal: Official statement of fiscal consequences (Executive Office of Administration and Finance): 'The proposed law may have an impact on state finances. CPCS receives its funding, in part, from state government appropriations. The fiscal impact of the proposed law is difficult to project due to the uncertainty regarding the outcomes of any such collective bargaining by CPCS employees.'

MA.title: State Primary Elections
MA.ballot_label: Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? This proposed law would eliminate political party primaries for state elections and instead establish a system where there would be a single, all-party primary in which all candidates, regardless of their party affiliation, would be listed on one ballot, and voters could vote for any candidate on the ballot. The two candidates receiving the most votes in the primary would advance to the general election ballot. This proposed law would require candidates for governor and lieutenant governor to run and be listed jointly on the ballot in the primary. This proposed law would provide political party status to any group whose candidates for any statewide office received at least 3% of the ballots cast in the state primary.
plain: Separate party primaries for state offices would end and be replaced by one primary that lists every candidate on the same ballot.
Any voter could vote for any candidate, and the two candidates with the most votes would move on to the general election.
Candidates for governor and lieutenant governor would run together on one line, and a group would gain party status if its statewide candidate won at least 3% of the primary vote.
MA.yes: A yes vote would eliminate separate party primaries for state elections and require a single primary in which all candidates appear on one ballot, voters could vote for any candidate, and the top two candidates would advance to the general election.
MA.no: A no vote would make no change to the laws governing primary elections.
MA.fiscal: Official statement of fiscal consequences (Executive Office of Administration and Finance): 'The proposed law has no discernible material fiscal consequences for state and municipal government finances.'

MA.title: Election Day Registration
MA.ballot_label: Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? This proposed law would permit eligible individuals to register to vote or update their voter registration address on Election Day. An individual who is eligible to vote could register to vote on Election Day by going to the polling place in the precinct where they live during voting hours and presenting proof of residency and signing a written oath. Proof of residency could be a valid photo identification, or documentation showing the individual's name and the address where the individual resides, such as a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, residential lease, wireless telephone statement, paycheck, current student fee statement or other document from a post-secondary school, or another government document or correspondence. The written oath would require the individual to certify that they are a citizen of the United States, are at least 18 years old, are not legally prohibited from voting, and have not and will not vote in the same election at another location. The oath would require the individual to acknowledge that providing false information is a felony punishable by not more than 5 years imprisonment or a fine of not more than $10,000, or both. If an individual did not present proof of residency, they would be allowed to cast a provisional ballot, which would be counted only if the individual returned to provide the required information before the close of polls for a municipal election; within two days after a state primary; or within six days after a state election. Individuals who register to vote on Election Day would be registered to vote in future elections as well as in the election taking place that day. Individuals who are already registered to vote would not be able to change their political party affiliation on Election Day. The proposed law would take effect on January 1, 2028.
plain: Eligible people could register to vote, or update their registration address, at their polling place on Election Day.
They would show proof of residency and sign a sworn statement, or cast a provisional ballot and supply the proof within a set number of days.
The change would take effect January 1, 2028, and people already registered could not switch political parties on Election Day.
MA.yes: A yes vote would permit eligible citizens to register to vote or to update their voter registration address at their polling place on Election Day.
MA.no: A no vote would make no change to the laws governing voter registration.
MA.fiscal: Official statement of fiscal consequences (Executive Office of Administration and Finance): 'The proposed law has no discernible material fiscal consequences for state and municipal government finances.'

MA.title: State Revenue Limit and Rebate
MA.ballot_label: Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? This proposed law would change the limit on how much revenue the state can collect in a given year. The proposal would limit state revenue in a given year to the net amount of state revenue from the year before, increased by a rate equal to the average growth of wages and salaries in Massachusetts over the most recent three years. If revenue collected by the state in a given year exceeds the limit, the excess amount would be refunded to taxpayers the following year. The proposed law would include all revenue from the surtax on incomes over $1 million when calculating the revenue limit and when determining whether state revenue exceeds the limit. The provisions of the proposed law would all be effective as of July 1, 2027. The proposed law states that, if any of its parts were declared invalid, the other parts would stay in effect.
plain: The yearly cap on state revenue would be set at the prior year's net revenue plus the average growth in Massachusetts wages and salaries over the last three years.
Any money collected above that cap would be refunded to taxpayers the following year.
Revenue from the surtax on income over $1 million would count toward the cap, and the change would take effect July 1, 2027.
MA.yes: A yes vote would change the limit on state revenue collection, tying it to prior year collections plus average wage and salary growth, and provide for a rebate of revenue exceeding that limit.
MA.no: A no vote would make no change in the law relative to state revenue collection.
MA.fiscal: Official statement of fiscal consequences (Executive Office of Administration and Finance): 'The proposed law would put stricter limits on allowable annual revenue growth available for budgeting. As a result, the proposal would reduce the amount of money available to support the state budget, which includes local aid for schools and municipal budgets. The proposal would also reduce the amounts available to build the state's Stabilization, or "rainy day," Fund - a reserve of money set aside to help Massachusetts manage economic downturns or emergencies without raising taxes or making major spending cuts. Depending on future conditions, the proposal could change the frequency of statutorily-required refunds to taxpayers.'

MA.title: Natural Resource Conservation Fund
MA.ballot_label: Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? This proposed law would establish a Nature for All Fund that, subject to appropriation by the Legislature, would receive 50% of state taxes collected from the sale and use of sporting goods, recreational vehicles, and golf courses for the first year of its operation. After July 1, 2028, the Nature for All Fund would begin receiving, subject to appropriation by the Legislature, 100% of state taxes collected on the sale and use of sporting goods, recreational vehicles, and golf courses. The sales tax revenue received by the Nature for All Fund would exclude sales tax revenue transferred to the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority State and Local Contribution Fund and the School Modernization and Reconstruction Trust Fund. The proposed law would allow the state Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs to spend the money in the Nature for All Fund for natural resource conservation. The proposed law would allow public and private donations to the Nature for All Fund. The proposed law would prevent the state comptroller from transferring surplus funds in the Nature for All Fund at the end of the fiscal year. It would also allow state agencies, municipalities, public charities involved in natural resource conservation, tribal governments, and other regional public entities to receive money from the Nature for All Fund. Natural resource conservation would include the conservation or restoration of land to protect drinking water, streams, rivers, lakes, coasts, farms, forests, connectivity between open spaces, and lands and natural resources of indigenous cultural significance. Natural resource conservation would also include the creation, improvement, and management of parks, trails, greenspaces or outdoor recreation access. The proposed law would establish a 15-member Nature for All Board that consists of five state officials and ten members of the public appointed by the Governor. The proposed law would require the ten members of the public to include representatives of underserved communities and indigenous peoples and at least one person with expertise or experience in natural resource conservation. The proposed law would allow the state Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs to spend money from the Nature for All Fund to hire staff to manage the fund. The proposed law would also require the Nature for All Board to establish rules about how the money in the Nature for All Fund should be spent, including rules regarding alignment with environmental justice principles, access to and restoration of lands and natural resources of indigenous cultural significance, promotion of affordable housing development, and other matters regarding spending and bond issuance. The proposed law would require the state Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs to submit an annual report to various state committees regarding the funds spent to buy or improve land in cities and towns containing environmental justice populations. The proposed law would take effect on July 1, 2027.
plain: A new Nature for All Fund would receive state sales and use tax money collected on sporting goods, recreational vehicles, and golf courses.
The fund would get half of that money in its first year and all of it after July 1, 2028, subject to appropriation by the Legislature.
A 15-member board would set the spending rules, and the money could pay for land and water conservation, parks, trails, and outdoor recreation access.
