MA.yes: A yes vote would create a fund that could be utilized for natural resource conservation that would receive some state taxes collected on the sale and use of sporting goods and recreational vehicles, and the use of golf courses.
MA.no: A no vote would not create this natural resource conservation fund or change how sales and use taxes are spent.
MA.fiscal: Official statement of fiscal consequences (Executive Office of Administration and Finance): 'The proposed law would have a significant impact on state and local budgets. While a full fiscal analysis is not feasible, it is estimated that, on an annual basis, the proposed law would automatically divert tens of millions of dollars of tax receipts that are currently supporting the state operating budget to the new fund. This proposed law would also have substantial implementation costs.'

MA.title: Single Family Homes
MA.ballot_label: Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? This proposed law would allow single-family homes to be built in a residentially zoned area as long as the land on which it is to be constructed is at least 5,000 square feet, has at least 50 feet of land bordering the street, road, or public way that it faces, and has access to public sewer and water services. The proposed law would allow cities and towns to reasonably regulate certain aspects of those single-family homes, including their height, distance from neighboring buildings, open space, parking requirements, and whether they can be rented out on a short-term basis. The proposed law would also allow the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities to issue guidance or regulations to administer the proposed law.
plain: Cities and towns would have to allow a single-family home on a residentially zoned lot of at least 5,000 square feet.
The lot would also need at least 50 feet of frontage on the street it faces and access to public sewer and water.
Local governments could still set reasonable rules on height, setbacks, open space, parking, and short-term rentals.
MA.yes: A yes vote would allow single-family homes to be built on lots of 5,000 square feet or more in residential areas, subject to reasonable local regulation of certain aspects of those homes.
MA.no: A no vote would make no change to the law relative to building single-family homes.
MA.fiscal: Official statement of fiscal consequences (Executive Office of Administration and Finance): 'If the proposed law enables the growth of housing in communities, it could provide positive new growth revenues to municipalities. However, it is difficult to project the potential scale of new growth tied to the proposed law. The proposed law thus has no discernible material fiscal consequences for state and municipal government finances.'

MA.title: Prohibit Retail Sale of Adult Recreational Use Marijuana
MA.ballot_label: Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? The proposed law would change the type and amount of marijuana that may legally be possessed in Massachusetts by repealing the laws that legalize, regulate, and tax the retail sale of adult recreational use marijuana in Massachusetts. The proposed law would also permit persons 21 years of age and older to possess 1 ounce or less of marijuana including no more than 5 grams in the form of concentrate, and to gift or transfer to another person 21 years of age and older 1 ounce or less of marijuana including no more than 5 grams in the form of concentrate. The proposed law would also impose a civil penalty of $100 and forfeiture of the marijuana for the possession of marijuana between the weight of 1 and 2 ounces. For persons 21 years of age and younger, the proposed law would make the possession of 2 ounces or less of marijuana a civil infraction subject to a $100 fine, forfeiture of the marijuana, completion of a drug awareness program and community service, and notification to their parents or legal guardian of the offense and penalties. The proposed law would allow currently licensed adult recreational marijuana businesses to apply on an expedited basis to become a licensed medical marijuana dispensary and to sell their remaining inventory of adult recreational marijuana to medical marijuana dispensaries. The proposed law would retain the Cannabis Control Commission but modify its authority so it would regulate only the medical marijuana market. The proposed law states that, if any of its parts were declared invalid, the other parts would stay in effect. The proposed law would take effect on January 1, 2028.
plain: The state laws that legalize, regulate, and tax retail sales of recreational marijuana would be repealed.
Adults 21 and older could still possess or give away up to 1 ounce, including up to 5 grams of concentrate, with a $100 civil penalty for 1 to 2 ounces.
Licensed recreational businesses could apply to become medical dispensaries, the Cannabis Control Commission would regulate only medical marijuana, and the change would take effect January 1, 2028.
MA.yes: A yes vote would prohibit the legalization, regulation, and taxation of the retail sale of adult recreational use marijuana, and change the penalties for possession of marijuana.
MA.no: A no vote would make no change to the law relative to marijuana.
MA.fiscal: Official statement of fiscal consequences (Executive Office of Administration and Finance): 'By repealing the laws that legalize and tax the retail sale of adult recreational use marijuana, the proposed law would reduce the amount that state and municipal governments receive from the taxation of those sales. In fiscal year 2025, taxation of the retail sale of adult recreational use marijuana raised approximately $280 million in state revenue and $50 million in local revenue. The state budget, which is supported by tax revenue, funds local aid for schools and municipal budgets.'

MA.title: Firearms Regulation
MA.ballot_label: Do you approve of a law summarized below, which was approved by the House of Representatives on July 18, 2024 by a vote of 124 to 33, and approved by the Senate on July 18, 2024 by a vote of 35 to 5? This law makes a number of changes to Massachusetts laws governing firearms. The law adds school administrators and licensed healthcare providers as parties permitted to ask a court to issue an Extreme Risk Protection Order - requiring an individual to surrender or relinquish their firearm licenses, permits, and firearms - if an individual is a present danger to self or others. The law also provides that, when issuing an Harassment Prevention Order, a court may also order the surrender of firearms licenses, permits, and firearms. The law imposes penalties for possessing, creating, and transferring untraceable "ghost gun" firearms and requires all firearms except antiques and relics, including unfinished frames and receivers that can be readily made into a finished product, to have serial numbers. The law includes privately-made guns like 3D-printed guns within the provisions governing untraceable "ghost gun" firearms. The law changes firearms licensing requirements to: (1) allow local licensing authorities to request prior license and permit information from the state, as well as access petitions for involuntary mental health commitments denied by a court in addition to prior involuntary commitments, as a part of their review of applications for licenses to carry firearms, firearm ID cards, and licenses to sell firearms; (2) require an individual to be 21 years of age to own semiautomatic rifles or shotguns; (3) add the possibility of incarceration of up to six months for a second offense of failing to report a firearm loss or theft; and (4) enable 12-15 year olds to apply for a self-defense spray permit with parental permission, and 15 to 18 year olds to apply independently. The law allows local firearm licensing authorities to transfer the responsibility to inspect firearm dealers to the State Police. The law requires local licensing authorities to attend statewide training regarding those inspections. It requires dealers to confiscate expired or suspended licenses and report them to the state and to local licensing authorities. The law changes the definition of "machine gun" to include bump stocks, trigger cranks, Glock switches and auto sears among the devices whose possession and use are subject to penalties. It expands the definition of "silencer" to include the parts used to construct a silencer. The law clarifies how to determine whether a firearm is an assault-style weapon and the circumstances under which a person may continue to possess assault-style weapons and large capacity feeding devices they already own. The law requires the state Firearm Control Advisory Board and the state Secretary of Public Safety and Security to review and update the rosters of prohibited assault-style firearms, approved firearms, and approved firearms sold for target shooting. The law clarifies requirements relating to the carry and transport of firearms in motor vehicles and ATVs. It prohibits the carrying of firearms in government buildings, polling locations, and schools, with certain exceptions. The law expands data compilation and reporting requirements to and from the state, and creates a publicly-accessible dashboard of anonymized aggregate firearm data, along with a commission to study that data. The law requires the State Police to provide training and a test for new applicants for licenses to carry or Firearm ID cards. The law establishes two special legislative commissions - one to examine funding for violence prevention services, and one to study emerging firearms technology. The law criminalizes discharging a firearm and striking a building in use.
plain: This is a referendum on a firearms law the Legislature passed in 2024, Chapter 135 of the Acts of 2024, known as An Act Modernizing Firearm Laws.

The law lets school administrators and licensed health care providers seek extreme risk protection orders, sets penalties for untraceable 'ghost guns', and requires a person to be 21 to own a semiautomatic rifle or shotgun.
It also broadens the legal definitions of machine gun and silencer and bars carrying firearms in government buildings, polling places, and schools, with some exceptions.
MA.yes: A yes vote would keep in place the law, which increases the regulation of firearms, including ghost guns, machine guns, and assault-style weapons.
MA.no: A no vote would repeal this law.
MA.fiscal: Official statement of fiscal consequences (Executive Office of Administration and Finance): 'Since the passage of this safety law in 2024, the Commonwealth has made significant investments to implement the law including training employees, promulgating new gun licensure processes, and developing IT infrastructure. Repealing the law would require the Commonwealth to expend resources in suspending or re-directing those investments.'

RI.title: Higher Education Facilities - $275,000,000
RI.ballot_label: Shall the action of the general assembly, by an act passed at the January 2026 session, authorizing the issuance of bonds, refunding bonds, and temporary notes of the State of Rhode Island for the capital projects and in the amount with respect to each such project listed below be approved, and the issuance of bonds, refunding bonds, and/or temporary notes authorized in accordance with the provisions of said act? Higher Education Facilities $275,000,000. Approval of this question will allow the State to issue general obligation bonds, refunding bonds, and/or temporary notes in an amount not to exceed two hundred and seventy-five million dollars ($275,000,000) for capital improvements to higher education facilities, to be allocated as follows: (a) University of Rhode Island Integrated Health Building $165,000,000 ... (b) RIC Adams Library Renovations $50,000,000 ... (c) CCRI Workforce Innovation Center $60,000,000 ...
plain: The state could borrow up to $275 million through general obligation bonds for public college and university buildings.
$165 million would build a new Integrated Health Building at the University of Rhode Island's Kingston campus.
$60 million would build a workforce innovation center at the Community College of Rhode Island's Warwick campus, and $50 million would renovate the Adams Library at Rhode Island College.
RI.yes: A yes vote authorizes the state to issue up to $275 million in general obligation bonds, refunding bonds, or temporary notes for these higher education projects.
RI.no: A no vote denies the state authority to issue these bonds, so the projects would not be funded this way.
RI.fiscal: The Rhode Island Senate Fiscal Office's FY2027 Budget as Enacted report states that Article 5 authorizes $600.0 million in bond referenda for the November 2026 ballot and that, assuming full issuance in bond year 1 at 5.0 percent interest, annual debt service is estimated at $48.1 million, with total debt service over the life of 20-year bonds of $962.9 million including $362.9 million in interest. That estimate covers all five questions together; a separate per-question debt service figure was not published in any source available as of September 22, 2026.

RI.title: Housing and Homeownership - $120,000,000
RI.ballot_label: Shall the action of the general assembly, by an act passed at the January 2026 session, authorizing the issuance of bonds, refunding bonds, and temporary notes of the State of Rhode Island for the capital projects and in the amount with respect to each such project listed below be approved, and the issuance of bonds, refunding bonds, and/or temporary notes authorized in accordance with the provisions of said act? Housing and Homeownership $120,000,000. Approval of this question will allow the State to issue general obligation bonds, refunding bonds, and/or temporary notes in an amount not to exceed one hundred and twenty million dollars ($120,000,000) to increase and preserve the availability of affordable and accessible housing to meet the needs of all Rhode Islanders and support community revitalization through the redevelopment of existing structures, new construction, property acquisition, and infrastructure improvements. Of this amount, at least twenty-five million dollars ($25,000,000) shall be allocated towards increasing production of housing intended for homeownership and up to ten million dollars ($10,000,000) may be used to support a program for public housing development.
plain: The state could borrow up to $120 million through general obligation bonds for affordable and accessible housing.
The money could pay for redeveloping existing buildings, new construction, buying property, and infrastructure improvements.
At least $25 million would go toward housing meant for homeownership, and up to $10 million could support a public housing development program.
RI.yes: A yes vote authorizes the state to issue up to $120 million in general obligation bonds, refunding bonds, or temporary notes for housing and homeownership programs.
RI.no: A no vote denies the state authority to issue these bonds, so these housing programs would not be funded this way.
RI.fiscal: The Rhode Island Senate Fiscal Office's FY2027 Budget as Enacted report states that Article 5 authorizes $600.0 million in bond referenda for the November 2026 ballot and that, assuming full issuance in bond year 1 at 5.0 percent interest, annual debt service is estimated at $48.1 million, with total debt service over the life of 20-year bonds of $962.9 million including $362.9 million in interest. That estimate covers all five questions together; a separate per-question debt service figure was not published in any source available as of September 22, 2026.

RI.title: Economic Development - $100,000,000
RI.ballot_label: Shall the action of the general assembly, by an act passed at the January 2026 session, authorizing the issuance of bonds, refunding bonds, and temporary notes of the State of Rhode Island for the capital projects and in the amount with respect to each such project listed below be approved, and the issuance of bonds, refunding bonds, and/or temporary notes authorized in accordance with the provisions of said act? Economic Development $100,000,000. Approval of this question will allow the State to issue general obligation bonds, refunding bonds, and/or temporary notes in an amount not to exceed one hundred million dollars ($100,000,000) to fund industrial facilities infrastructure improvements for economic development purposes to fund site development and growth industry infrastructure, to be allocated as follows: (a) Site Development $55,000,000 ... (b) Growth Industry Infrastructure $45,000,000 ...
plain: The state could borrow up to $100 million through general obligation bonds for economic development infrastructure.
$55 million would go to site development, including land purchase, environmental cleanup, utilities, the Quonset Business Park, and the I-195 District.
$45 million would support facilities and projects in ocean, defense, life sciences, and data analytics industries.
RI.yes: A yes vote authorizes the state to issue up to $100 million in general obligation bonds, refunding bonds, or temporary notes for site development and growth industry infrastructure.
RI.no: A no vote denies the state authority to issue these bonds, so these projects would not be funded this way.
RI.fiscal: The Rhode Island Senate Fiscal Office's FY2027 Budget as Enacted report states that Article 5 authorizes $600.0 million in bond referenda for the November 2026 ballot and that, assuming full issuance in bond year 1 at 5.0 percent interest, annual debt service is estimated at $48.1 million, with total debt service over the life of 20-year bonds of $962.9 million including $362.9 million in interest. That estimate covers all five questions together; a separate per-question debt service figure was not published in any source available as of September 22, 2026.

RI.title: Cultural Economy - $50,000,000
RI.ballot_label: Shall the action of the general assembly, by an act passed at the January 2026 session, authorizing the issuance of bonds, refunding bonds, and temporary notes of the State of Rhode Island for the capital projects and in the amount with respect to each such project listed below be approved, and the issuance of bonds, refunding bonds, and/or temporary notes authorized in accordance with the provisions of said act? Cultural Economy $50,000,000. Approval of this question will allow the State to issue general obligation bonds, refunding bonds, and/or temporary notes in an amount not to exceed fifty million dollars ($50,000,000) to provide funding for cultural economy efforts to be allocated as follows: (a) State History Center $45,000,000. Provides forty-five million dollars ($45,000,000) for the construction of a new Rhode Island State History Center. (b) State Preservation Grants Program $5,000,000. Provides five million dollars ($5,000,000) in matching grants administered by the Rhode Island Historical Preservation and Heritage Commission to cities, towns and nonprofit organizations for capital improvements to public historic sites, museums and cultural art centers located in historic structures, and heritage museums throughout the State.
plain: The state could borrow up to $50 million through general obligation bonds for cultural and historical projects.
$45 million would build a new Rhode Island State History Center.
$5 million would fund matching grants for cities, towns, and nonprofits to improve historic sites, museums, and cultural arts centers.
RI.yes: A yes vote authorizes the state to issue up to $50 million in general obligation bonds, refunding bonds, or temporary notes for a State History Center and historic preservation grants.
RI.no: A no vote denies the state authority to issue these bonds, so these projects would not be funded this way.
RI.fiscal: The Rhode Island Senate Fiscal Office's FY2027 Budget as Enacted report states that Article 5 authorizes $600.0 million in bond referenda for the November 2026 ballot and that, assuming full issuance in bond year 1 at 5.0 percent interest, annual debt service is estimated at $48.1 million, with total debt service over the life of 20-year bonds of $962.9 million including $362.9 million in interest. That estimate covers all five questions together; a separate per-question debt service figure was not published in any source available as of September 22, 2026.

RI.title: Green Economy Bonds - $55,000,000
RI.ballot_label: Shall the action of the general assembly, by an act passed at the January 2026 session, authorizing the issuance of bonds, refunding bonds, and temporary notes of the State of Rhode Island for the capital projects and in the amount with respect to each such project listed below be approved, and the issuance of bonds, refunding bonds, and/or temporary notes authorized in accordance with the provisions of said act? Green Economy Bonds $55,000,000. Approval of this question will allow the State to issue general obligation bonds, refunding bonds, and/or temporary notes in an amount not to exceed fifty-five million dollars ($55,000,000) for environmental and recreational purposes, to be allocated as follows: (a) Brownfields Remediation and Economic Development $3,000,000; (b) Facility Improvements $12,000,000; (c) Local Recreation Projects $1,000,000; (d) Marine Infrastructure Development $1,000,000; (e) Resilient Rhody Infrastructure Fund $25,000,000; (f) Narragansett Bay Watershed Restoration $7,000,000; (g) Agriculture Land Preservation Commission $3,000,000; (h) Open Space Program $3,000,000.
plain: The state could borrow up to $55 million through general obligation bonds for environmental and recreation projects.
$25 million would go to the Resilient Rhody Infrastructure Fund for resilience work, and $12 million would repair and build recreational facilities and parks.
Smaller amounts would fund brownfield cleanup, local recreation grants, marine infrastructure, Narragansett Bay watershed restoration, farmland preservation, and open space.
RI.yes: A yes vote authorizes the state to issue up to $55 million in general obligation bonds, refunding bonds, or temporary notes for these environmental and recreational purposes.
RI.no: A no vote denies the state authority to issue these bonds, so these projects would not be funded this way.
RI.fiscal: The Rhode Island Senate Fiscal Office's FY2027 Budget as Enacted report states that Article 5 authorizes $600.0 million in bond referenda for the November 2026 ballot and that, assuming full issuance in bond year 1 at 5.0 percent interest, annual debt service is estimated at $48.1 million, with total debt service over the life of 20-year bonds of $962.9 million including $362.9 million in interest. That estimate covers all five questions together; a separate per-question debt service figure was not published in any source available as of September 22, 2026.

VT.title: Proposal 3 - Right to collectively bargain (Article 23 of Chapter I)
VT.ballot_label: PROPOSAL 3. That Article 23 of Chapter I of the Vermont Constitution is added to read: Article 23. [Right to collectively bargain] That employees have a right to organize or join a labor organization for the purpose of collectively bargaining with their employer through an exclusive representative of their choosing for the purpose of negotiating wages, hours, and working conditions and to protect their economic welfare and safety in the workplace. Therefore, no law shall be adopted that interferes with, negates, or diminishes the right of employees to collectively bargain with respect to wages, hours, and other terms and conditions of employment and workplace safety, or that prohibits the application or execution of an agreement between an employer and a labor organization representing the employer's employees that requires membership in the labor organization as a condition of employment.
plain: The Vermont Constitution would say employees have a right to organize or join a labor union and bargain collectively through a representative they choose.
No state law could interfere with, cancel, or weaken that right over wages, hours, other job terms, or workplace safety.
No state law could block an agreement between an employer and a union that requires union membership as a condition of employment.
VT.yes: A yes vote adds this collective bargaining right to the Vermont Constitution.
VT.no: A no vote leaves the Vermont Constitution unchanged, with no constitutional right to collective bargaining.
VT.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate for this measure was published as of September 22, 2026; the Governor's proclamation and the Secretary of State's published notice contain no cost estimate.

VT.title: Proposal 4 - Equality of rights (Article 23 of Chapter I)
VT.ballot_label: PROPOSAL 4. That Article 23 of Chapter I of the Vermont Constitution is added to read: Article 23. [Equality of rights] That the people are guaranteed equal protection under the law. The State shall not deny equal treatment under the law on account of a person's race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, or national origin. Nothing in this Article shall be interpreted or applied to prevent the adoption or implementation of measures intended to provide equality of treatment and opportunity for members of groups that have historically been subject to discrimination.
plain: The Vermont Constitution would state that people are guaranteed equal protection under the law.
The state could not deny equal treatment under the law because of a person's race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, or national origin.
The amendment would not prevent programs meant to provide equal treatment and opportunity for groups that have historically faced discrimination.
VT.yes: A yes vote adds this equal protection guarantee to the Vermont Constitution.
VT.no: A no vote leaves the Vermont Constitution unchanged, with no such equal protection article.
VT.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate for this measure was published as of September 22, 2026; the Governor's proclamation and the Secretary of State's published notice contain no cost estimate.

FL.title: Budget Stabilization Fund
FL.ballot_label: CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT, ARTICLE III, SECTION 19. BUDGET STABILIZATION FUND.—Proposing an amendment to the State Constitution to increase the amount of funds that may be retained in the budget stabilization fund from 10% to 25% of general revenue collections, require the legislature to transfer the lesser of $750 million or the amount required to reach 25% of the general revenue collections each year unless certain conditions are met, and allow the legislature to withdraw funds for critical state needs.
plain: This amendment would let the state hold more money in its savings account, the Budget Stabilization Fund, by raising the cap from 10% to 25% of general revenue collections.
It would require the Legislature to deposit the lesser of $750 million or the amount needed to reach the 25% cap each year, unless certain conditions are met.
It would also let the Legislature take money out of the fund to pay for critical state needs.
FL.yes: A yes vote raises the Budget Stabilization Fund cap from 10% to 25% of general revenue collections, requires an annual deposit, and allows withdrawals for critical state needs.
FL.no: A no vote keeps the fund's cap at 10% of general revenue collections and leaves current deposit and withdrawal rules unchanged.
FL.fiscal: No Financial Impact Statement was published for this measure. Under Florida law the Financial Impact Estimating Conference prepares those statements for citizen initiatives only, and this is a legislative referral (HJR 5019, 2025 session). The Florida House's nonpartisan Final Bill Analysis states: "The fiscal impact on the state is indeterminate but likely insignificant."

FL.title: Exemption of Tangible Personal Property on Agricultural Land From Taxation
FL.ballot_label: CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT, ARTICLE VII, SECTION 3; ARTICLE XII. EXEMPTION OF TANGIBLE PERSONAL PROPERTY ON AGRICULTURAL LAND FROM TAXATION.—Proposing an amendment to the State Constitution to exempt tangible personal property habitually located or typically present on land classified as agricultural, used in the production of agricultural products or for agritourism activities, and owned by the landowner or leaseholder of the agricultural land from ad valorem taxation. If approved this amendment would first apply for tax years beginning January 1, 2027.
plain: This amendment would end local property taxes on equipment and other tangible personal property kept on land that is classified as agricultural.
The exemption would apply only to property used to produce agricultural products or for agritourism, and owned by the landowner or the person leasing the farmland.
If approved, the exemption would first apply to tax years beginning January 1, 2027.
FL.yes: A yes vote exempts qualifying farm and agritourism equipment and other tangible personal property on agricultural land from property taxes beginning with the 2027 tax year.
FL.no: A no vote leaves that equipment and other tangible personal property on agricultural land subject to local property taxes.
FL.fiscal: No Financial Impact Statement was published, because Florida prepares those only for citizen initiatives and this is a legislative referral (CS/HJR 1215, 2025 session). The Florida House Final Bill Analysis reports: "The Revenue Estimating Conference estimates that, if approved by the voters, the amendment proposed by the joint resolution will have a negative recurring impact on local government revenues of $31.0 million, beginning in Fiscal Year 2027-28."

FL.title: Increased Homestead Exemption; Lower Cap on Increases in Non-Homestead Property Assessments
FL.ballot_label: This amendment increases the homestead exemption, for all non-school taxes, to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and adjusts for inflation thereafter. It requires the Legislature to prescribe a uniform procedure for counties and municipalities, for their respective levies, to increase the homestead exemption up to full assessed value, and allows special districts, subject to referendum approval, to do the same. Persons who are not Florida residents on December 31, 2026, will receive the existing homestead exemption upon qualifying for a homestead exemption, with the increased homestead exemption beginning with the fifth year of exemption, to the extent permitted by the U.S. Constitution. This amendment reduces the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10% to 5%. This amendment requires counties and municipalities to use property taxes solely for public safety, education and schools, infrastructure, natural resources, bond debt service, retirement benefits for employees, and operations and administration. Other expenditures may be approved by county officers or county or municipal governing bodies unless prohibited by general law, notwithstanding Article VII, Section 9(a) of the Florida Constitution, which allows counties and municipalities to levy property taxes for their respective purposes. This amendment takes effect January 1, 2027.
plain: This amendment would raise the homestead exemption for all non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments after that.
It would lower the yearly cap on assessment increases for non-homestead property, such as rentals, vacation homes and commercial buildings, from 10% to 5%.
It would also limit counties and cities to spending property tax money on listed purposes such as public safety, schools, infrastructure, natural resources, debt payments and employee retirement.
FL.yes: A yes vote increases the non-school homestead exemption, lowers the non-homestead assessment cap to 5%, delays the larger exemption until the fifth year for people who are not Florida residents on December 31, 2026, and restricts how counties and cities may spend property tax revenue, all effective January 1, 2027.
FL.no: A no vote keeps the current homestead exemption amounts, the 10% cap on non-homestead assessment increases, and existing rules on how local governments may spend property tax revenue.
FL.fiscal: No Financial Impact Statement was published, because Florida prepares those only for citizen initiatives and this is a legislative referral (CS/HJR 1F, 2026 special session). The Florida House Final Bill Analysis estimates that, if approved, "the cash impacts on local non-school property tax revenues would be -$4.95 billion in Fiscal Year (FY) 2027-28 (with the $150,000 exemption in place) and -$8.78 billion in FY 2028-29 (with the $250,000 exemption in place). The recurring impact in all years is estimated to be -$11.86 billion on local non-school property tax revenues."

LA.title: Surviving Spouse of a Deceased Veteran with a Service-Connected Disability; One-Time Transfer of Additional Property Tax Exemption (Act 39, SB180)
LA.ballot_label: Do you support an amendment to allow the surviving spouse of a deceased veteran with a service-connected disability, who receives the additional property tax exemption, to make a one-time transfer of the additional property tax exemption to a subsequent qualifying property? (Effective January 1, 2027) (Amends Article VII, Section 21(K)(1))
plain: Louisiana gives an additional property tax exemption to veterans with a service-connected disability and to their surviving spouses.
This amendment would let a surviving spouse who already receives that additional exemption move it one time to a different qualifying home.
If approved, the change would take effect January 1, 2027.
LA.yes: A yes vote lets the surviving spouse of a deceased veteran with a service-connected disability transfer the additional property tax exemption one time to a later qualifying property.
LA.no: A no vote keeps the additional exemption attached to the property the surviving spouse currently claims, with no one-time transfer allowed.
LA.fiscal: Legislative Fiscal Office fiscal note (enrolled, 5/12/2026), coded "EN SEE FISC NOTE LF RV See Note": the measure "may result in a decrease in tax revenues" for local taxing bodies, but "the aggregate revenue impact is not expected to be significant." The note's baseline: 229 surviving spouses, roughly $1.6 million in exempt assessed value and about $168,000 in forgone revenue.

LA.title: Levy of a Lower Millage Rate Without Loss of Adjustment Authority (Act 273, HB521)
LA.ballot_label: Do you support an amendment to allow a local taxing authority to continue to levy a lower millage rate without losing its ability to adjust to the maximum authorized millage rate from a prior year's reassessment? (Effective January 1, 2027) (Amends Article VII, Section 23(C))
plain: When property is reassessed, a local taxing body may adjust its property tax rate, called a millage, up to a maximum allowed by law.
Under current rules, a body that chooses to keep charging a lower rate can lose the ability to move back up to that maximum later.
This amendment would let a local taxing authority keep levying the lower rate while preserving its ability to adjust to the maximum authorized after a prior reassessment.
LA.yes: A yes vote lets a local taxing authority levy a lower millage rate while keeping its ability to return to the maximum rate authorized from a prior reassessment, effective January 1, 2027.
LA.no: A no vote keeps current law, under which a taxing authority that levies below its maximum rate may lose the ability to adjust back up to it.
LA.fiscal: Legislative Fiscal Office fiscal note (enrolled, 5/12/2026), coded "EN SEE FISC NOTE LF RV See Note": the measure "may result in foregone ad valorem tax revenues," and "the extent of any decrease is indeterminable."

LA.title: Prohibition on Post-Conviction Bail for Aggravated Offenses Against a Minor Child (Act 271, HB51)
LA.ballot_label: Do you support an amendment to prohibit a defendant from being released on any post-conviction bail if the defendant is convicted of an aggravated offense against a minor child?  (Adds Article I, Section 18(C))
plain: After a conviction, a defendant can sometimes be released on bail while an appeal or further proceedings are pending.
This amendment would bar any post-conviction bail for a defendant convicted of an aggravated offense against a minor child.
The prohibition would be written into the bail section of the Louisiana Constitution.
LA.yes: A yes vote prohibits release on any post-conviction bail for a defendant convicted of an aggravated offense against a minor child.
LA.no: A no vote leaves the Constitution's bail provisions unchanged, so post-conviction bail remains available in those cases under existing law.
LA.fiscal: Legislative Fiscal Office fiscal note (enrolled, 5/17/2026), coded "EN SEE FISC NOTE LF EX": the measure "may result in an indeterminable increase in Local Funds expenditures for local governing authorities," and "The exact fiscal impact is indeterminable."

LA.title: Lifetime Limit on Election as Governor (Act 414, HB225)
LA.ballot_label: Do you support an amendment to prohibit a person who has served more than one and one-half terms as governor from being elected as governor for any future term? (Amends Article IV, Section 3(B))
plain: The Louisiana Constitution now bars a governor from being elected to more than two consecutive terms, but allows a former governor to run again after sitting out.
This amendment would bar anyone who has served more than one and one-half terms as governor from being elected governor in any future term.
That would turn the current limit on consecutive terms into a lifetime limit.
LA.yes: A yes vote bars a person who has served more than one and one-half terms as governor from being elected governor again at any future time.
LA.no: A no vote keeps the current rule, which limits consecutive terms but allows a former governor to run again after a break in service.
LA.fiscal: No fiscal note was published for this measure as of Sept. 22, 2026; the Legislative Fiscal Office issued no fiscal note on HB225.

LA.title: Application of Nonrecurring State Monies to Retirement System Unfunded Accrued Liability (Act 606, HB27)
LA.ballot_label: Do you support an amendment to authorize a state retirement system to apply any nonrecurring state monies it receives to any of its unfunded accrued liability rather than requiring application to its oldest unfunded accrued liability? (Amends Article VII, Section 10(D)(2)(b)(iii))
plain: State retirement systems sometimes receive one-time, nonrecurring state money to pay down pension debt.
Current rules require that money to be applied to the system's oldest unfunded accrued liability first.
This amendment would let a system apply that money to any of its unfunded accrued liability instead.
LA.yes: A yes vote lets a state retirement system apply nonrecurring state money to any of its unfunded accrued liability rather than requiring it go to the oldest debt.
LA.no: A no vote keeps the requirement that nonrecurring state money be applied to the system's oldest unfunded accrued liability.
LA.fiscal: No Legislative Fiscal Office fiscal note was published. The Legislative Auditor's enrolled actuarial note is coded "EN NO IMPACT APV" and states the legislation "is not expected to have any measurable effects on retirement related fiscal costs and revenues during the five-year measurement period."

LA.title: Additional Property Tax Exemption for Homeowners Age 65 or Older (Act 274, HB514)
LA.ballot_label: Do you support an amendment to authorize parishes and municipalities to extend an additional property tax exemption for property subject to the homestead exemption that is owned and occupied by a person who is at least sixty-five years of age and who qualifies for the special assessment level? (Effective January 1, 2028) (Adds Article VII, Section 21(P))
plain: Louisiana lets qualifying homeowners who are 65 or older freeze the assessed value of their home, a benefit called the special assessment level.
This amendment would let parishes and municipalities grant those homeowners an additional property tax exemption on their homestead.
If approved, the authority would take effect January 1, 2028.
LA.yes: A yes vote authorizes parishes and municipalities to grant an additional property tax exemption to homestead owners who are at least 65 and qualify for the special assessment level, beginning January 1, 2028.
LA.no: A no vote leaves parishes and municipalities without authority to grant that additional exemption.
LA.fiscal: Legislative Fiscal Office fiscal note (enrolled, 5/21/2026), coded "EN SEE FISC NOTE LF RV See Note": the measure "will result in an indeterminable but significant decrease in ad valorem tax revenues to local taxing authorities to the extent that the exemptions are approved through local elections." The note gives an illustrative statewide figure of roughly $19.4 million under a stated $1,000-per-property scenario.

LA.title: Public Funds for Drinking Water Utility Service Lines (Act 607, SB228)
LA.ballot_label: Do you support an amendment to allow for the use of public funds by a political subdivision for the purpose of identifying, inventorying, removing or replacing drinking water utility service lines made of or affected by materials as specified or prescribed by the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements of the United States Environmental Protection Agency, promulgated October 30, 2024, or subsequent promulgation, on property owned by utility customers? (Amends Article VII, Section 14)
plain: Some drinking water service lines that run to homes and businesses contain lead or other materials covered by federal drinking water rules.
The Louisiana Constitution generally bars spending public money on privately owned property, which can block local governments from replacing the customer-owned portion of those lines.
This amendment would let a parish, city or other political subdivision spend public funds to identify, inventory, remove or replace those covered service lines on property owned by utility customers.
LA.yes: A yes vote allows political subdivisions to spend public funds to identify, inventory, remove or replace covered drinking water service lines located on customer-owned property.
LA.no: A no vote keeps the constitutional restriction that bars spending public funds on that work on privately owned property.
LA.fiscal: Legislative Fiscal Office fiscal note (enrolled, 6/1/2026), coded "EN SEE FISC NOTE LF EX": the measure "may increase local fund expenditures for political subdivisions," with "no anticipated direct material effect on governmental revenues."

LA.title: Prohibition on Expropriation of Property by a Foreign Adversary (Act 277, HB192)
LA.ballot_label: Do you support an amendment to prohibit expropriation of property by a foreign adversary or an agent of a foreign adversary? (Amends Article I, Section 4(B)(4))
plain: Expropriation is the power to take private property for a public purpose, and the Louisiana Constitution sets out who may exercise it and on what terms.
This amendment would prohibit a foreign adversary, or an agent of a foreign adversary, from expropriating property in Louisiana.
The prohibition would be added to the property rights section of the state Constitution.
LA.yes: A yes vote prohibits a foreign adversary or an agent of a foreign adversary from expropriating property in Louisiana.
LA.no: A no vote leaves the Constitution's expropriation provisions as they are, with no express prohibition aimed at foreign adversaries.
LA.fiscal: No fiscal note was published for this measure as of Sept. 22, 2026; the Legislative Fiscal Office issued no fiscal note on HB192.

LA.title: Increase in the Income Limit for the Special Assessment Level (Act 220, HB300 of 2025)
LA.ballot_label: Do you support an amendment to increase the maximum amount of income a person may receive and still qualify for the special assessment level for residential property receiving the homestead exemption?  (Effective January 1, 2027)  (Amends Article VII, Section 18(G)(1)(a)(ii))
plain: Qualifying homeowners can freeze the assessed value of their homestead through the special assessment level if their income falls below a set limit.
This amendment would raise that income limit from $100,000 to $150,000 and delay the inflation adjustment of the limit from tax year 2026 to 2028.
If approved, the change would take effect January 1, 2027.
LA.yes: A yes vote raises the maximum income a homeowner may have and still qualify for the special assessment level on a homestead.
LA.no: A no vote keeps the current income limit for qualifying for the special assessment level.
LA.fiscal: Legislative Fiscal Office fiscal note (enrolled, 6/10/2025), coded "EN DECREASE LF RV See Note": "the bill can only serve to decrease ad valorem tax revenue collections," with the magnitude of the decrease stated to be undeterminable.

LA.title: Property Tax Exemption for Rehabilitated Blighted or Derelict Property (Act 272, HB214)
LA.ballot_label: Do you support an amendment to allow property tax exemptions for blighted or derelict properties that have been rehabilitated, and to require the legislature to enact laws providing for administration of these exemptions? (Effective January 1, 2027) (Adds Article VII, Section 21(P))
plain: Blighted or derelict properties are buildings that have fallen into serious disrepair or been abandoned.
This amendment would allow property tax exemptions for such properties once they have been rehabilitated.
It would also require the Legislature to pass laws setting out how those exemptions are administered, effective January 1, 2027.
LA.yes: A yes vote allows property tax exemptions for rehabilitated blighted or derelict property and requires the Legislature to enact laws administering them.
LA.no: A no vote leaves the Constitution without authority for a property tax exemption for rehabilitated blighted or derelict property.
LA.fiscal: Legislative Fiscal Office fiscal note (enrolled, 5/20/2026), coded "EN SEE FISC NOTE LF RV See Note": "The impact of the proposed exemption on local property tax revenues is indeterminable," with no material effect on expenditures.

VA.title: Proposed Constitutional Amendment, Question 1 (Right to Reproductive Freedom)
VA.ballot_label: Should the Constitution of Virginia be amended to (i) protect the freedom to make personal decisions about prenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care, birth control, abortion, miscarriage management, and fertility care; (ii) protect doctors, nurses, and patients from being punished for these decisions; and (iii) allow for restrictions on access to abortion during the third trimester of pregnancy except when the patient's health is at risk or the pregnancy cannot survive?
plain: This amendment would add to Virginia's Bill of Rights a right to make and carry out decisions about one's own reproductive care.

The protection would cover prenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care, birth control, abortion, miscarriage management and fertility care, and would shield patients and health care providers from penalties for those decisions.

The state could still regulate abortion in the third trimester, but any such law would have to allow abortion when it is medically needed to protect the patient's life or health or when the fetus is not viable.
VA.yes: A yes vote adds a right to reproductive freedom to the Virginia Constitution's Bill of Rights and limits when the state may restrict reproductive care.
VA.no: A no vote leaves the Virginia Constitution unchanged, so reproductive care remains governed by statutes that the General Assembly can change.
VA.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept. 22, 2026. Virginia's official explanation of a proposed constitutional amendment does not include a fiscal impact statement, and the Department of Elections published none for this question.

VA.title: Proposed Constitutional Amendment, Question 2 (Marriage)
VA.ballot_label: Should the Constitution of Virginia be amended to (i) remove the ban on same-sex marriage; (ii) affirm that two adults may marry regardless of sex, gender, or race; and (iii) require all legally valid marriages to be treated equally under the law?
plain: Virginia's Constitution still contains a provision barring marriage and civil unions between people of the same sex or gender, which court rulings have made unenforceable.
This amendment would remove that provision and state that two adults may marry regardless of sex, gender or race.
It would also require Virginia to recognize and treat all lawful marriages equally and bar denying a marriage license on those grounds.
VA.yes: A yes vote removes the same-sex marriage ban from the Virginia Constitution and requires equal legal treatment of all lawful marriages between two adults.
VA.no: A no vote leaves the existing constitutional ban on same-sex marriage in the text of the Virginia Constitution.
VA.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept. 22, 2026. Virginia's official explanation of a proposed constitutional amendment does not include a fiscal impact statement, and the Department of Elections published none for this question.

VA.title: Proposed Constitutional Amendment, Question 3 (Right to Vote; Qualifications of Voters)
VA.ballot_label: Should the Constitution of Virginia be amended (i) to provide for the fundamental right to vote in the Commonwealth, (ii) to revise the qualifications of voters so that a person convicted of a felony is not entitled to vote during his period of incarceration but is automatically invested with the right to vote upon release from incarceration, and (iii) to update the existing prohibition on voting by persons found to be mentally incompetent to instead apply to persons who have been found to lack the capacity to understand the act of voting?
plain: This amendment would state in the Virginia Constitution that voting is a fundamental right for qualified residents.
A person convicted of a felony could not vote while incarcerated but would get voting rights back automatically upon release, without having to ask the Governor for restoration.
It would also narrow the current bar on voting by people found mentally incompetent so that it applies only to people a court finds lack the capacity to understand the act of voting.
VA.yes: A yes vote makes voting a fundamental constitutional right, automatically restores voting rights when a person is released from incarceration, and narrows the mental-capacity disqualification.
VA.no: A no vote keeps current law, under which a felony conviction removes the right to vote until the Governor restores it individually, and the broader mental-incompetence disqualification remains.
VA.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept. 22, 2026. Virginia's official explanation of a proposed constitutional amendment does not include a fiscal impact statement, and the Department of Elections published none for this question.

WV.title: Citizenship Requirement to Vote in West Virginia Elections Amendment
WV.ballot_label: Summary of Purpose: "This amendment provides that in all elections held in West Virginia only citizens of the United States who are citizens of this state are qualified to vote." Constitutional text to be adopted: "Only citizens of the United States who are citizens of this state shall be entitled to vote at all elections held within the counties in which they respectively reside; but a person who is a minor, or who has been declared mentally incompetent by a court of competent jurisdiction, or who is under conviction of treason, felony or bribery in an election, or who has not been a resident of the state and of the county in which he or she offers to vote, for 30 days next preceding such offer, shall not be permitted to vote while such disability continues; and, a person in the military, naval, or marine service of the United States shall not be deemed a resident of this state by reason of being stationed therein."
plain: This amendment would change the West Virginia Constitution so that only United States citizens who are citizens of this state may vote in elections held in West Virginia.
It adds an explicit United States citizenship requirement to Article IV, Section 1, the section that lists who is qualified to vote.

It keeps the existing bars on voting by minors, people a court has declared mentally incompetent, people under conviction of treason, a felony or election bribery, and people who have not lived in the state and county for 30 days.
WV.yes: A yes vote writes a United States citizenship requirement for voting into Article IV, Section 1 of the West Virginia Constitution.
WV.no: A no vote leaves Article IV, Section 1 of the West Virginia Constitution as it reads now, without an explicit United States citizenship requirement.
WV.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate was published as of Sept. 22, 2026. The Secretary of State's July 23, 2026 public notice for this amendment contains no fiscal impact statement.

CA.ballot_label: Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance.

en: Lets the state borrow $11.25 billion by selling bonds.
Pays for rental housing, veterans’ home loans, supportive housing, and down-payment help.
The state pays it back over about 25 years.
es: Permite al estado pedir prestados $11.25 mil millones vendiendo bonos.
Paga vivienda de renta, préstamos para veteranos, vivienda de apoyo y ayuda para el enganche.
El estado lo paga en unos 25 años.

yes.en: The state could borrow $11.25 billion for veterans and affordable housing.
yes.es: El estado podría pedir prestados $11.25 mil millones para veteranos y vivienda asequible.

no.en: The state could not borrow that money.
no.es: El estado no podría pedir ese préstamo.

fiscal.en: About $500–600 million a year for about 25 years.
fiscal.es: Unos $500–600 millones al año por unos 25 años.

CA.ballot_label: Increases California’s Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns.

en: Makes the state’s savings account (the Rainy Day Fund) bigger: the cap rises from 10% to 20% of tax revenue.
Extends the state’s extra debt payments through 2040 instead of 2030.
The savings help keep schools, health care, and public safety funded when the economy is bad.
es: Hace más grande la cuenta de ahorros del estado (Fondo de reserva): el tope sube del 10% al 20% de los ingresos.
Extiende los pagos extra de deuda hasta 2040 en vez de 2030.
Los ahorros ayudan a mantener escuelas, salud y seguridad cuando la economía va mal.

yes.en: State reserves would be higher; extra debt payments continue longer.
yes.es: Las reservas serían mayores; los pagos extra de deuda durarían más.

no.en: Reserve and debt-payment rules stay the same.
no.es: Las reglas de reserva y pago de deuda siguen igual.

fiscal.en: State budget reserves would be higher.
fiscal.es: Las reservas del presupuesto estatal serían mayores.

title.es: Mantener impuesto a altos ingresos para escuelas

CA.ballot_label: Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education.

en: Keeps today’s higher income tax rates on people earning over $371,000 instead of ending them in 2031.
The money goes to public education and other programs.
The state keeps $5–15 billion a year it would otherwise lose.
es: Mantiene las tasas más altas de impuesto a quienes ganan más de $371,000 en vez de terminarlas en 2031.
El dinero va a educación pública y otros programas.
El estado conserva $5–15 mil millones al año que perdería.

yes.en: The 2012 tax increase on high earners becomes permanent.
yes.es: El aumento de impuestos de 2012 a altos ingresos se vuelve permanente.

fiscal.en: Keeps $5–15 billion a year in state revenue.
fiscal.es: Conserva $5–15 mil millones al año de ingresos estatales.

CA.ballot_label: Repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety.

en: Removes the ban on governments using public money for candidates’ campaigns.
State and local governments could choose to create public campaign funding programs, with limits.
Money set aside for education, transportation, or public safety could not be used.
es: Elimina la prohibición de usar dinero público en campañas de candidatos.
Los gobiernos estatal y locales podrían crear programas de financiamiento público, con límites.
No se podría usar dinero reservado para educación, transporte o seguridad.

yes.en: Governments could create public campaign financing programs.
yes.es: Los gobiernos podrían crear programas de financiamiento público de campañas.

fiscal.en: A few hundred thousand dollars a year for the state.
fiscal.es: Unos cientos de miles de dólares al año para el estado.

CA.ballot_label: Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment.

en: Changes what happens when a statewide officer, like the Governor, is recalled.
The recall ballot would only ask whether to remove them, not who replaces them.
The seat would be filled later by a special election or an appointment.
es: Cambia lo que pasa cuando se destituye a un funcionario estatal, como el Gobernador.
La boleta solo preguntaría si removerlo, no quién lo reemplaza.
El puesto se llenaría después por elección especial o nombramiento.

yes.en: Recall ballots no longer pick a replacement; vacancies are filled by special election or appointment.
yes.es: Las boletas de destitución ya no eligen reemplazo; las vacantes se llenan por elección especial o nombramiento.

no.en: Voters keep choosing the replacement on the recall ballot.
no.es: Los votantes siguen eligiendo el reemplazo en la boleta.

fiscal.en: Unknown; savings or costs of millions if a recall happens.
fiscal.es: Desconocido; ahorros o costos de millones si hay una destitución.

title.es: Préstamos para compradores de ingresos medios

CA.ballot_label: Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million.

en: Creates a state loan program for middle-income buyers of newly built homes under about $1.5 million.
The state could sell up to $25 billion in bonds; buyers get a fixed-rate loan for up to 17% of the price.
Homeowners’ loan payments pay the bonds back.
es: Crea un programa estatal de préstamos para compradores de ingresos medios de casas nuevas de menos de $1.5 millones.
El estado podría vender hasta $25 mil millones en bonos; el comprador recibe un préstamo fijo de hasta 17% del precio.
Los pagos de los propietarios devuelven los bonos.

yes.en: The state creates the program and can sell up to $25 billion in bonds.
yes.es: El estado crea el programa y puede vender hasta $25 mil millones en bonos.

fiscal.en: No direct state or local cost.
fiscal.es: Sin costo directo para el estado o los gobiernos locales.

CA.ballot_label: Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants.

en: Lets the state borrow $8.4 billion for immunology and immunotherapy research.
Half goes to one UC-affiliated research institute; half to research grants.
Paid back over about 20 years.
es: Permite al estado pedir prestados $8.4 mil millones para investigación en inmunología e inmunoterapia.
La mitad va a un instituto afiliado a la UC; la otra mitad a becas de investigación.
Se paga en unos 20 años.

yes.en: The state can borrow $8.4 billion for this research.
yes.es: El estado puede pedir prestados $8.4 mil millones para esta investigación.

fiscal.en: $500–600 million a year for about 20 years, partly offset if the research earns money.
fiscal.es: $500–600 millones al año por unos 20 años, en parte compensado si la investigación genera ingresos.

CA.ballot_label: Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification.

en: Requires a government-issued ID to vote in person.
Mail ballots would not count unless the last four digits of a government ID number are written on the envelope.
Today, your signature confirms your identity.
es: Exige identificación oficial para votar en persona.
Las boletas por correo no contarían sin los últimos cuatro dígitos de una identificación oficial en el sobre.
Hoy, tu firma confirma tu identidad.

yes.en: Voters must show extra ID each time they vote.
yes.es: Los votantes deben mostrar identificación adicional cada vez que votan.

no.en: Your signature keeps confirming your identity.
no.es: Tu firma sigue confirmando tu identidad.

fiscal.en: Tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
fiscal.es: Decenas a cientos de millones de dólares al año.

CA.ballot_label: Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care.

en: A one-time 5% tax on the wealth of people with assets over $1 billion.
Most of the money goes to health care.
The money is kept outside the usual school-funding and spending-limit rules.
es: Un impuesto único del 5% sobre la riqueza de quienes tienen más de $1 mil millones.
La mayor parte del dinero va a salud.
El dinero queda fuera de las reglas usuales de fondos escolares y límite de gasto.

yes.en: The state collects a one-time 5% wealth tax from billionaires.
yes.es: El estado cobra un impuesto único del 5% a los multimillonarios.

fiscal.en: Tens of billions in one-time revenue, spread over several years.
fiscal.es: Decenas de miles de millones en ingresos únicos, repartidos en varios años.

CA.ballot_label: Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes.

en: Cancels any new state tax passed after Jan 1, 2026 that keeps its money outside the state spending limit.
The State Auditor must review the programs a new special tax would fund before it reaches the ballot.
Programs paid for by special taxes get regular audits.
es: Cancela cualquier impuesto estatal nuevo posterior al 1 de enero de 2026 que quede fuera del límite de gasto.
El Auditor Estatal debe revisar los programas de un impuesto especial nuevo antes de la votación.
Los programas pagados con impuestos especiales tendrían auditorías regulares.

yes.en: New audits are required; new special taxes can’t be excluded from the spending limit.
yes.es: Se exigen auditorías nuevas; los impuestos especiales nuevos no pueden excluirse del límite de gasto.

no.en: Audit and spending-limit rules stay as they are.
no.es: Las reglas de auditoría y límite de gasto siguen igual.

title.es: Prohibir nuevos impuestos a bienes personales

CA.ballot_label: Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities.

en: Bans new state taxes on simply owning personal property, such as financial assets.
Bans new state taxes that reach back to past years.
Any conflicting tax passed after Jan 1, 2026 is cancelled.
es: Prohíbe nuevos impuestos estatales por solo poseer bienes personales, como activos financieros.
Prohíbe nuevos impuestos estatales retroactivos.
Cualquier impuesto en conflicto aprobado después del 1 de enero de 2026 se cancela.

yes.en: The state can’t create new taxes on owning financial assets or other personal property.
yes.es: El estado no puede crear nuevos impuestos por poseer activos financieros u otros bienes personales.

fiscal.en: Future tax revenue might grow less.
fiscal.es: Los ingresos futuros podrían crecer menos.

CA.ballot_label: Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027.

en: Raises the vote needed to pass voter-proposed local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds.
Applies to new, increased, or extended local special taxes starting Jan 1, 2027.
Some local taxes would be harder to pass.
es: Sube de mayoría a dos tercios el voto necesario para impuestos locales especiales propuestos por votantes.
Aplica a impuestos locales especiales nuevos, aumentados o extendidos desde el 1 de enero de 2027.
Algunos impuestos locales serían más difíciles de aprobar.

yes.en: Certain local taxes need two-thirds voter approval.
yes.es: Ciertos impuestos locales necesitan dos tercios de los votos.

fiscal.en: Local tax revenue might grow less.
fiscal.es: Los ingresos locales podrían crecer menos.

title.es: Regla de gasto para clínicas comunitarias

CA.ballot_label: Imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) that spend less than 90% of revenue on “program services” advancing their charitable purpose, including but not limited to patient services.

en: Requires nonprofit community health clinics to spend at least 90% of revenue on program services, including patient care.
Clinics that fall short face penalties.
The state’s new costs are covered by fees.
es: Exige que las clínicas comunitarias sin fines de lucro gasten al menos 90% de sus ingresos en servicios, incluida la atención a pacientes.
Las clínicas que no cumplan tendrían sanciones.
Los nuevos costos del estado se cubren con cuotas.

yes.en: Certain nonprofit clinics must spend 90% of revenue on services.
yes.es: Ciertas clínicas sin fines de lucro deben gastar 90% de sus ingresos en servicios.

fiscal.en: Low tens of millions a year for the state, covered by fees.
fiscal.es: Unas decenas de millones al año para el estado, cubiertas con cuotas.

CA.ballot_label: Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals.

en: Speeds up environmental review (CEQA) for most housing, transportation, water, and health projects.
Sets deadlines for finishing the review.
Sets deadlines for resolving lawsuits against project approvals.
es: Acelera la revisión ambiental (CEQA) de la mayoría de proyectos de vivienda, transporte, agua y salud.
Fija plazos para terminar la revisión.
Fija plazos para resolver demandas contra la aprobación de proyectos.

yes.en: Eligible projects get new, faster review and court procedures.
yes.es: Los proyectos elegibles tendrían procedimientos de revisión y judiciales más rápidos.

no.es: Los proyectos siguen con los procedimientos actuales.

fiscal.en: High tens of millions, possibly over $100 million, a year for governments.
fiscal.es: Decenas de millones, posiblemente más de $100 millones, al año para los gobiernos.

MT.notes: The Montana Secretary of State certified three citizen-initiated measures on 8/17/2026 (CI-132, CI-133, I-194). No legislative referendum (LR-) appears on the Secretary of State's list of issues qualified for the 2026 General Election ballot. The 2026 Montana Voter Information Pamphlet had not been posted at sosmt.gov/elections/vip/ as of Sept 22, 2026; that page still showed the 2024 pamphlet. Ballot language below is transcribed from the Secretary of State's official ballot-language PDFs.

NV.notes: The Nevada Secretary of State has published the official 2026 Statewide Ballot Questions guide (30 pages, issued by Secretary of State Francisco V. Aguilar). The guide states there will be only two statewide ballot measures this year and that there are no statewide Questions 1 through 5, because no petition circulated for 2026 gathered enough valid signatures. Both remaining questions are second-round votes under Article 19, Section 2 of the Nevada Constitution, which requires an initiated constitutional amendment to be approved at two successive general elections. A statewide initiative to exempt teachers and school staff from public-employee strike bans was withdrawn and is not on the ballot.

NM.notes: The New Mexico Secretary of State's official 2026 publication of statewide constitutional amendments and general obligation bond questions lists four constitutional amendments and three bond questions. Ballot text below is transcribed from that publication (English text; the same document also carries Spanish text). Fiscal figures come from the Legislative Finance Committee fiscal impact reports for the underlying joint resolutions.

UT.notes: Lieutenant Governor Deidre M. Henderson's 2026 General Election Certification, signed August 28, 2026, states that under Utah Code 20A-5a-209(2)(c) no statewide ballot propositions qualified for the 2026 Utah General Election ballot, and that the two proposed constitutional amendments below, passed by the Legislature, shall appear on the ballot. The H.B. 267 public-sector collective bargaining veto referendum had enough verified signatures but was removed from the ballot after the Legislature repealed H.B. 267 in the 2025 Second Special Session (approved December 11, 2025), eliminating the referendum's subject matter. A direct initiative to repeal the Independent Redistricting Commission and Standards Act did not gather enough signatures. Utah's 2026 Voter Information Pamphlet, which carries the Office of Legislative Research and General Counsel's impartial analysis and statement of fiscal effects, had not been published as of Sept 22, 2026.

WA.notes: Secretary of State Steve Hobbs certified three statewide measures for the November 3, 2026 general election: one Initiative to the People (IP26-645) and two Initiatives to the Legislature that the Legislature did not act on (IL26-001 and IL26-638). There are no advisory votes on the 2026 ballot; Washington abolished tax advisory votes with ESSB 5082 (Chapter 109, Laws of 2023). No statewide referendum or legislatively referred constitutional amendment was certified for 2026. Ballot titles are written by the Attorney General; fiscal impact statements are prepared by the Office of Financial Management under RCW 29A.72.025. The official voters' pamphlet components (ballot titles, explanatory statements, fiscal impact statements, arguments and rebuttals) were posted on the Secretary of State's site as of Sept 22, 2026; ballots are mailed to voters by October 16.

IN.notes: Indiana allows no initiatives or referendums; every statewide measure is a legislatively referred constitutional amendment. Indiana prints no separate title, summary, or fiscal estimate with a public question - voters see only the question text and 'YES'/'NO'. The 2026 Indiana Voter Information Guide published by the Secretary of State and Indiana Election Division (revised January 2026) does not describe the two public questions. The verbatim ballot text below was taken from an official Lake County, Indiana sample ballot for the November 3, 2026 general election and matches the joint-resolution text at the Indiana General Assembly.

IA.notes: Iowa has exactly one statewide measure. It is the only amendment on the Iowa Legislature's official Proposed Constitutional Amendment page that has completed both required passages ahead of the 2026 general election: HJR 2006 (90th General Assembly, final passage April 10, 2024) and SJR 11 (91st General Assembly, final passage May 3, 2026). The other item on that page, SJR 9 (91st G.A., 'Right of Accused to Confront Children and Other Witnesses'), has had only its first passage and is being published during 2026 ahead of a possible second passage; it is NOT on the 2026 ballot. Iowa's Secretary of State does not publish a statewide voter guide describing ballot measures. On county ballots the measure is designated 'Public Measure 1'; news coverage and campaigns commonly call it 'Amendment 1'.

KS.notes: Kansas has one statewide measure on the November 3, 2026 general election ballot. A second 2026 Kansas amendment, SCR 1611 (direct election of Kansas Supreme Court justices), was placed on the August 4, 2026 primary ballot and is therefore not a November measure. Kansas does not assign a number to ballot amendments; the ballot prints the proposition's title, an explanatory statement, 'vote for'/'vote against' statements, and the full text of the amendment.

MI.notes: Michigan's November 3, 2026 statewide ballot was finalized in early September 2026 with two statewide proposals. A third proposed constitutional amendment - the Americans for Citizen Voting proof-of-citizenship measure - will NOT appear: the Board of State Canvassers deadlocked over affidavits offered to cure signature problems and the Michigan Supreme Court declined to order it onto the ballot in early September 2026. The Board of State Canvassers approved the 100-word ballot summary for Proposal 2 on August 17, 2026, and a last-minute challenge to Proposal 2 failed at the Michigan Supreme Court the week of September 1, 2026. michigan.gov returned HTTP 403 to automated fetching, so the official ballot wording below was confirmed from Michigan public-media reporting of the Board of State Canvassers' approved language rather than read directly off the state page.

MN.notes: Minnesota has one proposed constitutional amendment on the November 3, 2026 ballot, authorized by 2026 Laws of Minnesota, Chapter 114. Minnesota does not number constitutional amendments on the ballot; the ballot prints a title and the question. The Attorney General has issued the statement of purpose and effect required by law. Under Minnesota law, leaving the question blank counts the same as a no vote, and the ballot carries that instruction.

MO.notes: Five statewide measures are certified for the November 3, 2026 general election: Amendments 3, 6, 7, and 8 and Proposition A. Four other measures (Amendments 1, 2, 4, and 5) were placed on the August 4, 2026 primary ballot and are not November measures. Missouri prints the Official Ballot Title and a Fiscal Note Summary on the ballot itself; the Secretary of State also publishes Fair Ballot Language for each measure. LITIGATION: (1) Amendment 3's ballot language was rewritten by the Missouri Court of Appeals in December 2025 after the court found the Secretary of State's version failed to tell voters it would repeal the 2024 reproductive-rights amendment; the rewritten language is what is certified. (2) Amendment 6 was declared insufficient by Secretary of State Denny Hoskins on Aug. 4, 2026 and struck from the ballot by Cole County Circuit Judge Daniel Green on Aug. 19, 2026 on single-subject grounds, but the Missouri Supreme Court reversed on Sept. 3, 2026 and ordered it certified for the November ballot under the ballot title certified in September 2025. (3) Proposition A, the veto referendum on the 2025 mid-decade congressional map, was upheld by the Missouri Supreme Court on Sept. 3, 2026; separate federal litigation over WHICH congressional map Missouri must use in 2026 was still active as of Sept. 22, 2026 (Justice Kavanaugh denied a stay Sept. 8; the U.S. Supreme Court stayed a conflicting federal district court order Sept. 10; the Eighth Circuit ruled Sept. 21 and stayed its own ruling for a week pending further U.S. Supreme Court review). That federal fight concerns the map used for the 2026 congressional elections, not whether Proposition A appears on the ballot.

NE.notes: Secretary of State Robert B. Evnen certified the 2026 general election ballot on Sept. 11, 2026. Four statewide measures: three citizen initiatives (440, 441, 442) plus one constitutional amendment referred by the Legislature (LR19CA). The SoS 'Informational Pamphlet on Initiative Measures' covers only 440-442; LR19CA is posted separately as an Executive Board-approved ballot statement. Nebraska does not publish an official fiscal note for ballot measures. A fourth initiative (the 'Respect Nebraska Voters' / four-fifths-vote proposal) was removed from the ballot by the Nebraska Supreme Court on Sept. 10, 2026 for violating the single-subject rule and is NOT on the ballot.

ND.notes: Exactly two statewide measures are on the Nov. 3, 2026 general election ballot per the Secretary of State's measures page and the official 'Analyses of the Statewide Measures' publication required by N.D.C.C. 16.1-01-07. Two other legislature-referred measures did not reach this ballot: a single-subject constitutional measure was voted on at the June 9, 2026 primary, and a term-limits measure (SCR 4008, 2025) was ordered off the November ballot by the North Dakota Supreme Court on June 25, 2026.

SD.notes: Four statewide ballot questions, all constitutional amendments referred by the Legislature in 2025. No initiated measure or initiated amendment qualified by petition for this ballot, and no referred law appears among the certified questions (a referendum petition on SB 245 was approved for circulation on 4/29/2026 but is not listed among the certified ballot questions). Titles, explanations and the effect of a Yes/No vote are written by the Attorney General; the Secretary of State's 2026 Ballot Question Pamphlet also carries proponent and opponent statements.

OH.notes: Exactly one statewide issue is certified for Nov 3, 2026: State Issue 3. There are no statewide Issues 1 or 2 this cycle; no citizen-initiated statewide measure (including proposals on property taxes and on data centers) qualified for the 2026 ballot, per reporting on the Ohio Ballot Board's Aug. 3, 2026 meeting. The Ohio Ballot Board certified the Issue 3 ballot language, certified explanation, and arguments for and against on Aug. 3, 2026 (announced by the Secretary of State on Aug. 18, 2026), so issue numbering is final. Ohio's 2026 congressional redistricting is not the subject of any statewide measure on this ballot. NOTE ON SOURCING: ohiosos.gov blocked all automated retrieval (HTTP 403) during this research, so the certified Ballot Board text could not be read in full; the enrolled joint resolution text below was retrieved directly from the Ohio Legislature's document service and is verbatim.

WI.notes: Three statewide constitutional amendment questions are certified for Nov 3, 2026 - this year Wisconsin's questions are on the November ballot, not the spring ballot. Each cleared two consecutive legislatures: first consideration by the 2023 legislature (2023 Enrolled Joint Resolutions 16, 11, and 15) and second consideration by the 2025 legislature (2025 SJR 116, 2025 AJR 10, and 2025 AJR 102 respectively). Question text, explanatory statements, and resolution numbers below were read verbatim from the official statewide Type C Notice of Referendum Election for November 3, 2026.
