The Wisconsin Elections Commission's own copy of that notice (source_url) returned HTTP 403 to automated retrieval on 2026-09-22; the identical notice was read in full from the City of Franklin, Wisconsin clerk's posting of the same WEC-issued document.

CT.notes: No statewide ballot question is certified for November 3, 2026. The only live amendment vehicle in the 2026 session was SJ 37, a resolution proposing an environmental rights amendment; it was reported favorably out of the GAE Committee on March 20, 2026 and placed on the Senate calendar (File No. 510), but it never got a floor vote in either chamber before the session adjourned on May 6, 2026, so it did not reach the required three-fourths vote. Connecticut's automatic constitutional-convention question is not due before 2028 (last submitted in 2008). Caution: the Secretary of the State's ballot-question page is stale and still displays November 6, 2018 materials, so it does not affirmatively confirm either way; confirmation came from the General Assembly bill-status record at https://www.cga.ct.gov/asp/cgabillstatus/cgabillstatus.asp?selBillType=Bill&bill_num=SJ00037&which_year=2026.

DE.notes: No statewide ballot measure is certified for November 3, 2026. Delaware is the only state that amends its constitution without a popular vote (two-thirds approval by two successive General Assemblies), and it has no initiative or referendum process, so statewide ballot questions are very rare. The Department of Elections links to the text of proposed constitutional amendments at https://legis.delaware.gov/docs/default-source/default-document-library/153rdgaconstamendtextfinal.pdf, but those are enacted by the General Assembly and do not go to voters.

ME.notes: No statewide ballot measure is certified for November 3, 2026. The Legislature referred no bond issues or constitutional amendments to this ballot. One citizen initiative ('An Act to Designate School Sports Participation and Facilities by Sex') was found to have enough signatures in March 2026, but on May 26, 2026 Secretary of State Shenna Bellows determined after review that only 67,150 signatures were valid, short of the 67,682 required, and the initiative was removed. Sponsors had a 10-day right to appeal that decision; the final outcome of any appeal could not be confirmed.

MA.notes: Nine questions were certified on July 21-22, 2026 - the most since 1994. All nine are citizen-initiated (eight initiative petitions plus one veto referendum). The official 'Information for Voters' guide (88 pages) was published and mailed to households in mid-September 2026. On the printed ballot each question is headed only 'Question N - Law Proposed by Initiative Petition' (or 'Referendum on an Existing Law' for Question 9); the short titles below are the ones used in the Information for Voters guide, not on the ballot itself. Questions 1-8 share the preamble: 'Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026?' Each question carries an official fiscal statement of no more than 100 words prepared by the Executive Office of Administration and Finance under M.G.L. c. 54, s. 53.

NJ.notes: No statewide public question is certified for November 3, 2026. The Department of State's official 2026 election information page lists candidates, certifications and the 11th Congressional District special election, but no public questions, bond acts or amendments. Several constitutional amendment resolutions were introduced in the 222nd Legislature (SCR 30, 35, 68, 74 and 106; ACR 50) but none was agreed to by both houses, and New Jersey's roughly three-month pre-election publication deadline (about August 3, 2026) passed with nothing filed.

NY.notes: No statewide ballot proposal is certified for November 3, 2026. The State Board of Elections website is bot-protected and returned HTTP 403 to automated requests, so confirmation came from county sample ballots (for example Ulster County's November 3, 2026 sample ballots list only town and village propositions, and a statewide proposal would have to appear on every county ballot). The five ballot proposals New York City voters will see are City Charter amendments and are local, not statewide. Date trap: search engines frequently surface two Article 8 amendments (small-city school district debt limits and a sewage facilities extension) as current; those were November 2023 Proposals 1 and 2. New York's November 2025 Proposal 1 was the Mount Van Hoevenberg Olympic Sports Complex Adirondack Park land amendment, which passed.

PA.notes: No statewide ballot question is certified for November 3, 2026. Article XI of the Pennsylvania Constitution requires identical joint resolutions to pass in two consecutive legislative sessions and then requires the Secretary of the Commonwealth to advertise the amendment in each of the three months before the election. A text scan of every weekly Pennsylvania Bulletin issue from July 4 through September 19, 2026 (volumes 56-27 through 56-38, at https://www.pacodeandbulletin.gov/secure/pabulletin/data/vol56/) found no proposed constitutional amendment or ballot question notice, so the August and September advertising windows elapsed empty and no amendment can reach this ballot. SB 251 (childhood sexual abuse statute of limitations) remains stalled without second passage. Ballot questions appearing in Philadelphia and other municipalities in 2026 are local Home Rule Charter questions.

RI.notes: Five general obligation bond questions totaling $600 million were referred to voters in Article 5 of the FY2027 state budget (H. 7127, Substitute A, as amended), signed by Governor Dan McKee on June 12, 2026. Article 5 lists the projects in this order: (1) Higher Education Facilities $275,000,000; (2) Housing and Homeownership $120,000,000; (3) Economic Development $100,000,000; (4) Cultural Economy $50,000,000; (5) Green Economy Bonds $55,000,000. Section 2 of Article 5 directs the Secretary of State to prepare ballot labels for each project with 'approve' or 'reject' next to it. The Secretary of State's final question numbering (Question 1 through Question 5) could not be confirmed from an official source, because the Voter Information Center site (vote.sos.ri.gov) blocked automated access; the measures below are listed in the order set out in the enacted act. Publication of the 2026 Voter Information Handbook could not be confirmed for the same reason.

VT.notes: Two legislatively referred constitutional amendments are on the ballot. Governor Phil Scott formally proclaimed on July 28, 2026 that Proposals 3 and 4 will be voted on at the general election on November 3, 2026, as required by Section 72 of Chapter II of the Vermont Constitution and Chapter 32 of Title 17 of the Vermont Statutes Annotated. Vermont does not mail a statewide voter guide; the Secretary of State publishes notice of the proposals in print and on the websites of the General Assembly and the Secretary of State. The ballot_label text below is the amendment language exactly as it appears in the Governor's official proclamation; the exact heading formatting used on the printed ballot was not confirmed. Both proposals are drafted as a new 'Article 23' of Chapter I.

FL.notes: All three measures are legislative referrals; no citizen initiative qualified for 2026. Florida requires 60% approval for passage. Amendment 3's ballot title and summary were rewritten under court order: on Aug. 4, 2026 a Leon County circuit judge ruled the Legislature's title ('Save Our Homes From Excessive Property Taxes') and summary misleading, and the Attorney General filed revised language on Aug. 13-14, 2026. The 'ballot_label' for Amendment 3 below is the revised text carried by the Division of Elections; Amendments 1 and 2 use the Legislature's original enrolled ballot statements, which were not challenged.

LA.notes: Louisiana votes on constitutional amendments on its own schedule, and 2026 has two amendment elections. Five amendments referred by the 2025 Legislature were voted on at the MAY 16, 2026 statewide election (originally set for April 18, 2026 and moved by Act 2 of the 2025 First Extraordinary Session); those are not included here. Ten amendments are set for NOVEMBER 3, 2026: nine acts of the 2026 Regular Session plus HB300 of the 2025 Regular Session (Act 220). One further 2026 act, SB68 (Act 38, Louisiana Supreme Court discipline of out-of-state attorneys), specifies the April 17, 2027 election and is NOT on the November 2026 ballot. Ballot text below is quoted verbatim from each enrolled act on legis.la.gov. IMPORTANT: the Secretary of State had not published its 'Statement of Proposed Constitutional Amendments' for Nov. 3, 2026 as of Sept. 22, 2026, so the official amendment NUMBERS are not confirmed; the 1-10 ordering used here comes from two independent news listings that agree with each other, and should be re-checked against the Secretary of State once published. Also note a drafting collision: Amendment 10 (Act 272) and Amendment 6 (Act 274) both add Article VII, Section 21(P).

MS.notes: No statewide ballot measures. The Mississippi Secretary of State's official statewide sample ballot for the Nov. 3, 2026 general election (dated 9/9/2026) contains only federal, special legislative/district attorney, and nonpartisan judicial contests, and ends with 'END OF BALLOT' with no measure section. Mississippi has had no functioning citizen initiative process since the state Supreme Court invalidated it in 2021, and efforts to restore it failed again in the 2026 session. No legislatively referred amendment completed the required two-thirds passage for the 2026 ballot.

SC.notes: No statewide ballot measures. South Carolina has no citizen initiative or veto referendum process; amendments reach voters only by joint resolution passed by two-thirds of each house. A review of the 2025-2026 session's ratified acts and joint resolutions found no joint resolution proposing a constitutional amendment for submission to the electors. The one constitutional item, S. 582 (Act No. 245), is a ratification of the amendment voters already approved at the 2024 general election, not a new ballot question. The S.C. Election Commission's election listings for Nov. 3, 2026 show no statewide ballot question.

TX.notes: No statewide ballot measures. Texas votes on constitutional amendments in odd-numbered years, because the Legislature meets in regular session only in odd-numbered years. The 89th Legislature's 17 proposed amendments were all submitted at the Nov. 4, 2025 constitutional amendment election. The Secretary of State's election law calendar describes Nov. 3, 2026 as the uniform general election date for federal, state and county officers, with no statewide propositions, and the Legislative Reference Library lists no constitutional amendment election for 2026. Local political subdivisions may still place local bond or other propositions on this date.

VA.notes: Three proposed constitutional amendments are on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot. A fourth proposed amendment, on congressional redistricting, was decided at a separate special election earlier in 2026 and is not on the November ballot. The Virginia Department of Elections publishes an official explanation for each question prepared under Va. Code Sec. 30-19.9; ballot text below is quoted from those official pages.

WV.notes: Secretary of State Kris Warner issued the official Public Notice on July 23, 2026 for one proposed amendment, designated Amendment 1. A second proposed amendment to raise the homestead exemption (HJR 42) did NOT make the ballot: the House passed it March 4, 2026, the Senate amended it March 13, and the House never acted on the Senate amendment before the session ended, so it failed. West Virginia amendments pass by simple majority.
